News.title: Serial sex predator Simon Levy guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London
News.content:
Serial sex predator Simon Levy guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London

Serial sex predator Simon Levy, 40, has been found guilty at the Old Bailey of murdering two women and raping a third in London

View 4 Images Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo (left) and Sheryl Wilkins were killed in March and August respectively (Image: PA)

A serial sex offender has been found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third woman in London.

Simon Levy, 40, was convicted of the murder of Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, and Sheryl Wilkins, 39. He was also convicted of two counts of rape, assault occasioning grievous bodily harm (GBH) with intent and non-fatal suffocation over a brutal sex attack in January 2025, which the victim survived.

Levy, from Tottenham, north London, murdered Ms Valencia-Trujillo in March last year, and Ms Wilkins in August last year.

Ms Valencia-Trujillo was found dead at a property on the Aylesbury estate in south-east London on March 17, while Ms Wilkins was found unresponsive in High Road, Tottenham, on August 24.

View 4 Images Court artist sketch of Simon Levy (Image: PA)

Several months earlier, in January last year, Levy carried out a violent sex attack on a woman in a car park in Tottenham in which her collarbone was broken, the Old Bailey heard.

He pleaded not guilty to the two women’s murders and further denied two charges of rape, grievous bodily harm with intent, and non-fatal suffocation against the surviving woman.

Prosecutor Tom Little KC told the court that Ms Valencia-Trujillo was found in a block of flats that is “very largely disused” with few residents or passers-by except security guards.

View 4 Images Sheryl Wilkins, 39, was killed in August last year (Image: Metropolitan Police/PA Wire)

Levy travelled to the area the day before and killed her during the course of a sexual encounter. Mr Little said: “The position her body was left in is similar to that of the other murder.”

Levy is a serial sex offender

His trial at the Old Bailey, which began in late June, heard Levy had been convicted of around 13 sexual assaults committed since July 2018.

Prosecutors said he is a serial predator who agreed to pay the women for sexual activity before killing them.

Jurors heard Levy has previous convictions for sexual assault, six of which happened in the same time period.

The murder of Sheryl Wilkins took place in the same car park in Tottenham where the surviving woman was allegedly attacked.

View 4 Images Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, died in the Aylesbury Estate in south-east London on March 17 (Image: PA)

Levy declined to give evidence at trial

At the conclusion of the prosecution case, Judge Mark Lucraft KC asked Levy’s defence lawyer, Siobhan Grey KC, if he would be giving evidence.

She replied that he had declined the opportunity and confirmed Levy had been advised that jurors could draw inferences from his failure to do so.

The defence then called forensic pathologist Dr Brett Lockyer, who the court heard had advised on television programmes such as Silent Witness.

After a review of post-mortem examination findings, Dr Lockyer agreed the cause of the women’s deaths was “unascertained”, which he said was relatively rare in forensic work.

Giving evidence about Ms Valencia-Trujillo’s death, he said the body being face down “complicated” matters, especially when there was a suggestion of possible neck compression.

The pathologist told the jury that injuries including petechial haemorrhaging, congestion of the face, froth in the airway and injury to the neck are not necessarily significant on their own, but taken together they can “build a picture” to suggest a victim was strangled.

Article continues below

The “hallmark” injury in strangulation cases is damage to the voicebox or the bone that sits above the voicebox, he said, and this is sometimes only visible under a microscope.

News.title: M6 traffic: Motorway closed in West Midlands with lorry on fire
News.content:
Images show plumes of smoke coming from a lorry fire on the M6 northbound - between J4A for the M42 and J5 for Castle Bromwich - which forced the carriageway to close

M6 traffic: Motorway closed in West Midlands with lorry on fire

Motorists are facing delays on a major motorway following a lorry fire.

Images show plumes of smoke which rose on the M6 northbound between J4A for the M42 and J5 for Castle Bromwich. The incident caused tailbacks of nine miles and 90 minute delays.

The carriageway was blocked with emergency services at the scene including West Midlands Fire Service.

National Highways states: "Traffic is stopped on the #M6 northbound in the #WestMidlands between J4 #BirminghamAirport & J6 #Birmingham due to a HGV fire. @WestMidsFire are working on scene. Current delays of up to 90 minutes on the approach, with 9 miles of congestion."

News.title: Exact ages people make their biggest life changes as Brits say they’re more ambitious than ever
News.content:
Exact ages people make their biggest life changes as Brits say they’re more ambitious than ever

Four in 10 say they are more ambitious than ever while 85% are currently working towards a major life goal

View 2 Images Rochelle Humes at the launch of Vodafone's Opportunity Hub, which has been created to provide tools, technology and advice (Image: Vodafone)

Brits are making major life changes in their 30s and have bigger plans for the future than ever, according to new research. The average person now moves abroad at 31, switches career at 32, starts a business at 33 and launches a side hustle at 34.

‌



Four in 10 say they are more ambitious than ever while 85% are currently working towards a major life goal, according to the study by Vodafone.

‌



But despite this, people wait an average of two years before acting on their ambitions, leaving 20% feeling a twinge of regret and admitting they wish they had acted sooner.

‌



Financial constraints (22%) emerged as the biggest barrier holding people back, with a lack of confidence or self-belief (15%), lack of time (13%), fear of failure (12%) and limited access to resources or tools (9%) also preventing people from getting started.

A major life event often provides the push people need to pursue long-held ambitions. For those who said a life experience was the biggest catalyst, the most common were bereavement (27%), losing a job or being made redundant (25%) and becoming a parent (25%).

More broadly, other triggers include realising life is too short to keep waiting (26%), achieving greater financial stability (23%) and feeling more confident (22%).

‌



The research also shows how central technology has become in helping people turn ambition into action with 42% believing improved connectivity has helped them achieve their goals.

More than half (55%) say it is now easier to find opportunities thanks to digital tools, while 49% believe they are better placed to achieve their ambitions today than they were five or ten years ago.

To help people turn "one day" into today, Vodafone opened the UK's first Opportunity Hub, a space designed to provide the tools, technology, advice and connections needed to unlock opportunity.

‌



View 2 Images Anne Whitehouse speaks at the launch (Image: Vodafone)

Speakers at the event included Rochelle Humes, with Roman Kemp, alongside journalist, author and social advocate, Anna Whitehouse, and executive coach and psychotherapist David Waters and content creator and entrepreneur, Jade Beason.

Experts from Enterprise Nation and Vodafone also shared practical advice and support, helping attendees turn their ambitions into reality.

‌



A VodafoneThree spokesperson says: “Britain isn't short of ambition. The challenge is turning ambition into action. Our research shows that connectivity is increasingly part of that equation, with nearly two-thirds of would-be founders saying unreliable connectivity has held them back from starting a business locally.

“That's why we're investing in initiatives like The Opportunity Hub and our £11billion plan to build the UK's best network. Because when people have access to the right support and connectivity, they're better placed to seize new opportunities and achieve their goals.”

Just as The Opportunity Hub helps individuals unlock their potential, this nationwide investment will unlock growth, inspiration and digital confidence for millions across the UK, ensuring people have the connectivity they need to achieve whatever comes next.

Article continues below

If you’d like to find out more about VodafoneThree’s commitment to building the UK’s best network and how its £11bn investment is creating opportunity across the UK, visit: Home - Building the UK's Best Network | VodafoneThree .

News.title: Vladimir Putin has backed himself into a corner as prodding NATO may have dire consequences
News.content:
Against a backdrop of his failing and disastrous war in Ukraine, it is difficult to imagine why President Vladimir Putin would further test NATO with an attack.

Russia is suffering a catastrophically-hit economy, dire recruitment issues, an ill-disciplined and incompetent military and losses to death and injury of some 1.4 million troops.

But Kremlin doctrine and Putin’s nature dictates that retreat is not an option, given the poor optics that would deliver back home and abroad and there are rumblings of dissent in Moscow. The way he probably views his situation is as if he is backed into a corner even though this position is all of his own making.

Now there are reports Putin could attack a NATO ally within weeks to put the alliance to the test and many in the intelligence community are concerned this could happen. Poland and the Baltic States have warned for months that Moscow could launch an attack, some even suggesting the Kremlin would try a ‘false flag’ assault.

‌



But the latest reports are far more serious and indicate Putin may even give the go-ahead for an attack involving Russian troops, although it is unclear exactly where. Sadly, whilst it is impossible to read Putin’s mind, judging by his past actions it is possible something exasperating and escalatory like this could happen.

Ukraine and Europe developing new major new missiles capable of smashing Russia's ballistic threat READ MORE :

Major Russian airport used by millions every year evacuated in urgent missile alert READ MORE :

View 3 Images Russian President Vladimir Putin with his navy and submarine (Image: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputni)

Testing NATO’s resolve, reaction times, cohesion, military organisation and determination to thwart his expansion plans are essential to maintaining what he believes is leverage. He wants to know what he can get away with without poking NATO so hard that Russia will suffer consequences beyond sanctions and diplomatic furore.

Reports suggest a major cyber attack is possible, since there would be an element of deniability but actions on the ground such as an incursion are also a possibility. We only have to look at how Putin’s Russia has behaved in recent years to judge what they are capable of. His special forces have murdered people on British streets in the Salisbury attack of 2018, the 2006 poisoning of former spy Alexander Litvinenko in London.

‌



His regular troops have committed countless war crimes, including rape, torture, murder and kidnapping in Ukraine. Russian mercenary networks such as The Wagner Group have committed heinous acts across Syria, Africa and beyond. But beyond sanctions and the banishing of scores of his declared spies he has not suffered hard, overt military consequences from his actions, apart from support for Ukraine.

NATO countries are pumping vast resources into the war in Ukraine, an arms race is underway following the US’s insistence Europe has to learn to defend itself against Russia. This has triggered the Kremlin into action, regardless of the fact it was Russia’s invasion of Ukraine that prompted NATO’s urgent re-arming and not a threat from the alliance.

View 3 Images Britain's Defence Secretary Wes Streeting shakes hands with acting Minister of Defence of Ukraine Yevhenii Khmara (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

Ukraine and Europe developing new major new missiles capable of smashing Russia's ballistic threat READ MORE :

And many believe it is entirely possible he has for the past four years been misled into believing his war in Ukraine is progressing far better than it actually is. Several years ago during a meeting with a former CIA officer I asked him how Putin would react to an embarrassing rumour that was emerging about his health.

‌



The retired spook told me: “It is very possible he is unaware of it - who among the sycophants he has surrounded himself with would want to tell him? They could easily end up falling out of a window. That’s what happens to despots - they often don’t get bad news because everyone is too nervous to pass it on. Even worse, their underlings get used to telling the boss what they believe he wants to hear, constantly agreeing with the person and never arguing.”

The pressure Putin perceives from NATO’s support of Ukraine is entirely of his own doing, as is the European arms race to prepare for a perceived threat from Russia. Putin has isolated himself so much he may not know exactly how badly the war is going for Russia. An armed provocation on Polish soil or elsehwhere would tell him exactly what those consequences would be and he may think he can get away with it, to keep pushing and prodding.

The momentum towards Kremlin aggression towards Eastern Europe is almost unstoppable since his stated aim is to re-create the Soviet empire. And that is why, until NATO lashes out physically the Russian bully will keep poking and provoking until he gets a punch on the nose - and the outcome of that will be either the end of his presidency or a wider war.

News.title: Man in 70s dies after plunging 'considerable distance' down Cumbria waterfall
News.content:
Man in 70s dies after plunging 'considerable distance' down Cumbria waterfall

Emergency services and rescue teams were called to Moss Force in the Lake District but the man was pronounced dead due to his injuries

View Image The Moss Force waterfall in the Newlands Valley in the Lake District (file) (Image: Tripadvisor)

Emergency services and rescue teams were called to a popular spot in the Lake District after a man fell down a waterfall.

‌



The incident took place as the man "had slipped and fallen a considerable distance" down Moss Force near Newlands Hause in Cumbria at around 2.40pm on Sunday.

‌



Members of the public rushed to help before the emergency services arrived.

‌



Mountain rescue teams, an air ambulance, the police and the fire service were sent to the scene but the man was pronounced dead due to his injuries.

A statement released this morning by Keswick Mountain Rescue Team reads: "A multi-agency response was initiated following a report that a man had slipped and fallen a considerable distance down Moss Force near to Newlands Hause.

‌



"Visitors to the waterfall, including off duty medical professionals, provided initial support whilst emergency services made their way to the scene. Sadly, despite the best efforts of all involved, the man died as a result of his injuries.

"Our thoughts and condolences go out to the man’s family and friends." A spokesperson for Cumbria Police confirmed the man was in his 70s and that there are no suspicious circumstances surrounding the death.

A statement from the source reads: "Police were called at 2:38pm on the 2 August 2026 to reports of a man that had fallen near Moss Force. Emergency services responded to the scene.

Article continues below

"Despite the best efforts of members of the public, North West Ambulance Service and North West Air Ambulance, a man in his 70s was sadly declared deceased. There are no suspicious circumstances.

"A file will be prepared for the coroner."

News.title: 'I sold Andy Burnham his £80 T-shirt, here is the key detail everyone got wrong'
News.content:
While the Labour Party revels in the ‘Burnham bounce,’ the manufacturer of the Prime Minister’s favourite clothes is enjoying the best free advertising it’s ever had. For when doubters criticise Andy Burnham for spending £80 on a T-shirt or £295 on a pair of jeans, Manchester’s Private White V.C’s sales rocket.

As the former Mayor of Manchester vows to “bring back hope,” the 150-year-old business, responsible for the understated quality of the PM’s wardrobe, has its own campaigning motto - ‘saving Britain, one raincoat at a time.’ Mocking the PM - although she undoubtedly envies his approval ratings and probably his style - Kemi Badenoch dubbed him “a pair of eyelashes and a black T-shirt.”

Andy Burnham given rockstar welcome to Number 10 North by Mancunian fans READ MORE :

But, as James Eden, CEO of Private White V.C, the great grandson of the brand’s founder, Private Jack White V.C - a First World War hero - made clear to The Mirror, it’s actually very dark navy and is no ordinary black T-shirt. Whenever Mr Burnham pops into their Manchester store, as he did last Saturday to buy their wool peacoat, he is buying a beautifully crafted garment, made using fine British fabric.

View 8 Images Private White V.C. CEO James Eden with Prime Minister Andy Burnham

‌



The PM also owns their £695 Harrington jacket, £295 jeans and a made-to-measure suit - all paid for himself. And, with his salary boosted from £118,267 as Mayor of Manchester to £174,039 as Prime Minister, James, 43, a former investment banker, hopes he will be buying a lot more.

He says: “Andy’s been a fan and loyal supporter of our brand for three years now. There have been no freebies - he has purchased all his pieces himself."

The company’s red brick mill, which steps off the River Irwell, in Salford, just north of Manchester City centre, is in an area steeped in industrial history, just a 26 minute walk from Heron House, the new No10 North.

View 8 Images Private Jack White V.C., who won the Victoria Cross for bravery

‌



James, who lives in nearby Altrincham with his wife and three children, describes the PM’s most recent half hour visit, saying: “He drank builders’ tea and ate chocolate Hobnobs and Jaffa Cakes, while picking out pieces. He’s the most authentic man. He’s incredibly proud to be Mancunian and keen to support our local British brand.”

Marketing executive Harrison Heaton, 21, agrees, saying: “You wouldn’t think you were serving the man in charge of the country, he’s so down to Earth. And he certainly looks good in our clothes.”

The deeds to the Private White V.C. mill date back to 1853, but the brand’s story began with Jack White V.C. A private in the First World War, Jack won the Victoria Cross by jumping into a river under heavy machine-gun fire in 1917, tying a copper telephone wire to his boat and towing it to safety after everyone else in the vessel was killed or wounded.

View 8 Images The Private White V.C. factory in Salford, steps from central Manchester

‌



James adds: “We include copper detailing on a lot of our clothes as a nod to his bravery.” Mr Burnham’s Harrington jacket, for example, which he wore to celebrate his win in Makerfield, has a copper zip.

When Jack returned to civilian life, he was employed as an apprentice at his local raincoat factory in Salford, training as a pattern cutter. He became factory supervisor, general manager and, eventually, factory owner.

After his death in the 1940s, the business moved through different guises and family members. And in 1996, aged 13, James began working in the factory to earn some summer money. He says: “At the time, the factory was a private label company, making garments for ostensibly the best brands in the world. As an impressionable teenager, I was always quite seduced by the Burberry check or Aquascutum patterns.”

View 8 Images Getting measured for his suit - Andy Burnham at the Private White V.C. factory

‌



Upstairs, in the tardis-like mill, an archive room houses one of almost every garment made in the factory over the years. During our tour, James showed me a coat the factory made for the World Cup winning England National Team in 1966, dubbed the Ramsey Raincoat.

But James worked in banking during his 20s, surviving the 2008 financial crash, but taking redundancy in 2012 and investing in the factory - switching things up to make their own label garments, instead of manufacturing clothing for other quality brands.

And so, the Private White V.C. of the modern age was born. The Mancunian menswear label now employs more than 100 people and has dressed celebrities including David Beckham, Liam Gallagher, Tom Hardy and Pierce Brosnan. James notes: “We make custom clothes for women too, and Princess Anne is a fan.”

View 8 Images Princess Anne is a fan of Private White V.C., who make custom clothes for women too

‌



Entering the mill through a large red door, a stylish ground floor shop has lured in customers including the Eagles, Coldplay and Daniel Craig. There’s a large floor-to-ceiling Victor comic, depicting Jack’s First World War heroics in cartoon form.

A wartime trench coat stands proudly on a mannequin, oil marks still present at the bottom. James says: “That coat has seen some things. It was made for the Allied forces in the Second World War.”

Burnham’s Harrington jacket is displayed nearby, next to a poster emblazoned with the brand’s ‘saving Britain, one raincoat at a time’ motto.

James says: “The story of our Harrington begins in World War II when Winston Churchill called for a fabric to protect downed RAF pilots in freezing waters. You land in the water, you get wet, you get cold, you’ve had it. The result was Ventile [a 100% cotton, high density fabric] invented in Manchester, down the road at The Shirley Institute in Didsbury. It remains unmatched today.” The Harrington is seamed with copper, to avoid water being let in by minute stitch holes.

‌



View 8 Images Victor comic cover: “The Real Story of a Man at War Private White V.C."

In the belly of the factory upstairs, Derek Hughes, 65, a fabric cutter who has been with the brand for 26 years, says: “We’re a family and very proud of what we produce.” In the centre of the floor, two 100-year-old Manchester-made cutting machines are still used today.

All the clothes are cut, stitched and finished by hand. Private White V.C.’s garments are made on site, using 90% locally sourced materials (with the exception of Scottish cashmere and Swiss hardware). James says: “We are a true British brand and a circular economy, buying from local businesses.”

He shows off a reel of wool used to make a coat worn by Ethan Hawke. The label reads “woven in Delph, Oldham, Lancashire”. Explaining why their clothes are expensive, James says: “We pay for the best materials - and source them locally.

‌



View 8 Images Hollywood actor Ethan Hawke in his Private White V.C. coat

“We pay our workers well, and as a result there are people who have been with the brand for decades. You’re not paying for a machine to mass produce a garment, you’re paying a highly skilled artisan to make something by hand. We don’t compromise on materials, on yarns, on labour.”

James hopes Mr Burnham who has been to the store about half a dozen times, will spur others to buy from them. He says: “We currently export more clothes than we sell here in the UK. Our biggest market is the US, who seem to have a greater appreciation for British clothing than the Brits do. We’d love for that to change.

“If people spent their money on British brands, it would boost the economy, increase opportunity. We have such a rich history of textiles in this country and we are incredibly proud to be flying the flag.”

‌



*For more information see privatewhitevc.com

News.title: Serial sex offender guilty of murdering two women and raping third
News.content:
A serial sex offender who was being monitored by the Metropolitan Police has been found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third in London.

Simon Levy killed Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, in March 2025 and 39-year-old Sheryl Wilkins five months later.

The 40-year-old also raped a third woman in January 2025 in the same Tottenham car park where Wilkins was later found dead.

During his trial at the Old Bailey, jurors heard Levy had been convicted of several sexual assaults dating back to July 2018, including one carried out against a prison officer in 2022.

News.title: How police let a registered sex offender murder and attack women
News.content:
His first victim was attacked was on a busy Tube in central London.

Levy boarded and positioned himself directly in front of the woman, before leaning his elbow on her. She moved away.

A few minutes later, she felt something touch her, over her clothes, on her vagina. Such was the force Levy used, that she felt like it was an attempt to push his fingers inside her through clothing.

She grabbed Levy's hand and asked what he was doing, but he did not respond.

When other passengers asked if she was alright, Levy protested his innocence.

"What are you talking about - look my hand is covered," he said, pointing to the jumper draped over his arm.

Levy then called her "crazy" and "stupid" and got off the tube at Westminster Station.

The woman got off at the next stop, upset and crying.

She went on to report the assault to BTP. There was CCTV available of Levy, but police did not identify him. He would only be linked to the case two years later, after more women had been attacked.

A year after his first Tube assault, he assaulted three more women in quick succession and was arrested.

After being assaulted herself, the first of those three victims then filmed Levy sexually assaulting a second, unidentified woman, travelling in the same carriage.

The first woman immediately reported what had happened to BTP and provided the footage. Levy assaulted a third woman a week later.

After he had been questioned and had denied the three offences, BTP officers said they did not have enough evidence to charge, and he was released on bail.

The subsequent British Transport Police investigation was full of delays. It was weeks before identity parades were arranged, and BTP did not approach the CPS for six months.

When it did, in May 2025, a CPS team had to scramble to make an emergency charging decision overnight, because BTP had again arrested Levy and wanted him in court the next day. This was highly unusual - BTP had known about the initial offences for six months.

In a statement, BTP Assistant Chief Constable Charlie Doyle said: "It is clear that opportunities to expedite the investigation were missed and we have amended our procedures to address these issues to ensure that repeat offenders are dealt with expeditiously and that linked offences are prioritised more effectively."

News.title: Cambridge to review process for hiring senior academics after Jason Arday resignation
News.content:
A group of academics is calling for an independent investigation into the appointment of Jason Arday, who resigned from his University of Cambridge roles following allegations of plagiarism.

The professor of education has also faced accusations of fabricating or exaggerating elements of his CV. He has defended himself and his work.

Attention has now turned to Cambridge's handling of concerns about Arday, who became its youngest-ever black professor in 2023, as well as his upcoming memoir.

Cambridge said findings from an investigation into Arday's academic qualifications and appointments would "feed into" a new review on the appointment process for senior academic roles.

The university said on Friday that it would "continue to investigate the circumstances around Jason Arday's appointment and tenure". A spokesperson declined to comment further when approached by the BBC.

Priyamvada Gopal, professor of postcolonial studies at Cambridge and among those calling for an independent probe, said the university was facing "massive reputational damage" over the affair.

"This is reputational damage that has upset colleagues across disciplines, across the political spectrum," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Friday.

"I've been quite struck by the number of people who are very upset by what has happened. So I don't think it is an option for Cambridge to just sweep this under the carpet and not take any action at all."

Cambridge announced on Wednesday that it had begun an investigation into "new information" about Arday's academic qualifications and appointments, having already said it was looking into allegations of plagiarism.

But Gopal said the university should not be "marking its own homework", adding that the group of academics of which she is a part had suggested a mix of senior academics at Cambridge and elsewhere to conduct an investigation.

Accusations of plagiarism in Arday's work were first voiced by Nathan Cofnas - a US researcher whose role at a Cambridge college was terminated after backlash against his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".

He highlighted that plagiarism detection software had found several tracts of Arday's PhD dissertation to be copied verbatim or lightly rephrased from prior academic works by other authors.

Liverpool John Moores University (LJMU), which awarded Arday's PhD, has said it investigated the allegations of plagiarism last year and dismissed them, saying they were likely the result of "honest and reasonable error".

It told the BBC on Friday that its position remains unchanged in light of recent events and that his PhD "still stands".

Cofnas also noted that a retired professor had previously raised concerns about Arday's subsequent academic articles, which led to two journals issuing correction notes, and raised questions about some of his claimed achievements, including extensive marathon running and raising millions for charity.

Several universities at which Arday claimed on his CV to have had academic positions have since denied him having those roles.

The controversy has attracted a range of opinions, including within academia, about whether he had been scrutinised unfairly because of his race.

Arday has admitted errors in his work but denied plagiarism, saying his autism and a lack of adequate supervision early in his academic career may have contributed to those mistakes. He also denied lying about his achievements.

He said his decision to step down should not "be mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me", which he has previously said were "racially motivated".

Gopal said universities were "being targeted in particular by a lazy and false division between academic excellence and diversity and equality on campus", which was "really part of culture wars rather than any part of university life".

She and her colleagues found it "unusual" that Arday had been appointed to a "very senior, very prestigious" post early in his career - and that he had been put forward in the media with "frankly a bit of a target on his back".

Gopal also said any investigation should review "whether the university was involved in any way or any level with efforts to deter journalists from reporting on the allegations".

This came after it emerged the Metropolitan Police investigated Times Higher Education (THE) reporter Jack Grove over a complaint of harassment after he contacted Arday concerning allegations of plagiarism last year.

The Telegraph also reported that Arday hired law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to THE which implied that the "apparent attack" on Arday might be "racially motivated".

The Met closed the case and Commissioner Sir Mark Rowley apologised for the investigation, telling LBC on Thursday that the complaint should have been "screened out earlier on as not requiring investigation".

News.title: Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Breakfast on Friday, former Det Sup Blaik, who led the Thames Valley Police investigation, pointed to remarks by the judge who sentenced PC Harper's killers. Mr Justice Edis referred to their case of manslaughter as being "very close to a case of murder in its seriousness".

The former officer called for prisoners who were judged to have had a high level of culpability for a manslaughter offence to be excluded from the scheme.

Allowing them to walk free would "undermine" the judicial process and impact police morale, Blaik said, before urging the government to have a "long, hard think" about the case.

The former Det Sup left Thames Valley Police in 2023. This is the first time he has publicly shared his views on the issue.

In an earlier statement given exclusively to BBC Breakfast, he said "like many people across the country" he was "deeply concerned and appalled" by the prospect of Bowers and Cole being considered for early release.

He said that because the "death of Andrew was such a serious and tragic case", Bowers and Coles should "not be afforded the opportunity" to be released early.

"Neither of them showed any remorse during their time in police custody or during their subsequent trial.

"I hope the Government takes account of the strength of public feeling on this issue, which has been both clear and widespread," he added.

Under revised plans announced by the government on Monday, prisoners who have committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences will be excluded from an early release scheme for England and Wales.

But those guilty of manslaughter may still be eligible.

An average of 150 people a year are sentenced at crown court for manslaughter with an average term of nine years. That means that in any given year there are hundreds of these offenders in jail. If they were all kept in, that would eat into the available spare beds - a number that is declining despite the massive prison-building programme.

If the government were to try to differentiate between different types of manslaughter offenders based on the specific nature of the crime they committed, that could be legally complex to deliver - and may in turn face serious legal challenges from prisoners who find their release dates changed.

Bowers and Cole were sentenced to 13 years for the manslaughter of PC Harper.

They will become eligible for release from prison after serving half of their sentences under the plans, instead of two-thirds.

The driver of the getaway car, Henry Long, was jailed for 16 years for the same offence. But Long will not be eligible.

News.title: England footballer Ivan Toney charged with assault at Soho nightclub
News.content:
England footballer Ivan Toney has been charged with assault at a nightclub in central London.

The 30-year-old, who plays for Saudi Pro League club Al-Ahli, was charged on 31 July following an incident on Wardour Street in Soho on 6 December.

The former Brentford striker, who started England's 6-4 win over France in the "bronze final" of the World Cup last month, has been charged with assault causing actual bodily harm and is due to appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on 24 September.

A spokesperson for Toney said: "Ivan acknowledges the charge and although he is naturally shocked, he looks forward to being given the opportunity to clear his name in court."

After starting his career at Northampton Town, the striker had permanent spells at Newcastle, Peterborough and Brentford before moving to Saudi Arabia in 2024.

He was a surprise selection for England's World Cup squad but apart from the France game, his only other appearance was as a late substitute in the 2-1 semi-final defeat to Argentina.

News.title: How a 90-second power outage sparked  chaos for rail commuters
News.content:
The power failure which hit a Network Rail operations centre in Manchester was a rare incident.

But after commuters were left facing chaos, it has raised questions about how a short outage at one operating centre could have a widespread impact.

Network Rail will face scrutiny for how its systems coped and responded to the outage.

That's the publicly-owned body whose job it is to operate and maintain Britain's railway infrastructure. That means the tracks, signals, embankments and major stations.

It was at Network Rail's operating centre in Manchester that the problem started. Its operating centres are where crucial controls are housed that let trains run safely across the country, with Manchester's centre responsible for large parts of the North West.

It was hit by a power cut in the area, which was resolved within 90 seconds. And despite having a backup supply, given the centre's importance, this failed to kick in as quickly as expected.

Because signalling was affected - think of that as the traffic lights of the railway - trains had to stop.

Systems had to be rebooted. But there was some damage to the systems controlling signalling, and that took time to fix because of the need to replace certain parts.

Thinking about how busy parts of the rail network are, and how many trains and crews were left out of position across the North West of England and beyond, helps explain why the impact was so big.

Network Rail has apologised to customers and opened an investigation.

Bosses say engineers have been working hard to "build additional resilience into our signalling systems to ensure that this doesn't happen again".

News.title: Data breach investigation into Minnie Merriman's medical records
News.content:
NHS Tayside is investigating an alleged data breach into the medical records of a nine-year-old girl at the centre of a murder probe in Arbroath.

Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, died at Ninewells Hospital in Dundee after being found seriously injured at an industrial estate in the town.

Her father has appeared in court charged with her murder.

NHS Tayside said it was "investigating the circumstances" of the alleged breach that happened in a clinical area where staff access patient information.

A spokesperson added: "As a matter of governance, any data protection breach would be recorded and investigated by NHS Tayside and, where appropriate, reported to the Information Commissioner's Office (ICO).

"It would not be appropriate for us to comment further on individual staffing matters."

News.title: Madonna and Blur producer William Orbit dies aged 69
News.content:
Acclaimed British music producer William Orbit, known for his work with acts including Madonna, Blur, All Saints and U2, has died at the age of 69.

A statement released on Friday by Orbit's family and friends "with profound sadness" said he died at home on 23 July. No cause of death was given.

"He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched through his music, friendship and kindness," the statement said.

North London-born Orbit, who real name was William Wainwright, helped to reinvigorate Madonna's career in 1998 with the album Ray of Light, which blended electronic dance music and ambient techno with pop and trip-hop.

It went on to win three Grammy Awards and remains, for many people, the Queen of Pop's greatest record.

News.title: Brothers jailed for killing man and injuring his son while racing cars home
News.content:
Following sentencing, Rhys' wife Caroline Jenkins, also known as Carrie, said in a statement she often wondered what difference it would have made to her family's future "if we'd hugged a little tighter and a little longer" when she waved them off that day.

She said, for her son, life "without a dad who was involved in everything you did is a hard adjustment" and it "carried an element of PTSD".

Carrie said Ioan was emotionally and physically scarred by the crash.

"It's impossible to convey the full impact Rhys' death had on us," she said, and there remains a "massive hole left in our lives by his unnecessary death".

Ioan, who broke both arms, and suffered a fractured rib and perforated bowel, said he wished his dad was still here to "watch me grow up and be my dad".

Rhys' youngest son, Gruff, was six when the crash happened.

In his own victim impact statement, he said he was in bed when police arrived to tell his mum what had happened.

After being told his dad had died, he said: "I ran out of the house. I didn't know where I was going. It was the worst feeling of my life."

The court was told Umar Ben Yusaf's car was not directly involved in the crash, but the "competitive" nature of his driving with Abubakr Ben Yusaf contributed significantly.

Judge Timothy Petts said the trauma the Jenkins family had been through in the last 21 months was "difficult for me to summarise".

"You have all been suffering with your own devastating grief but also trying to deal with the practical consequences of Rhys's death and Ioan's injuries.

"It has been an horrendous time for all of you," he told them.

Petts said to Umar and Abubakr Ben Yusaf that he was satisfied they were racing each other.

"Both of you were constantly riding your luck at high speed, completely unnecessarily, and eventually it ran out with appalling consequences.

"Rhys Jenkins never stood a chance because you were so close to him when you lost control. He was driving perfectly properly and did nothing wrong. He had no time to avoid the collision."

Sgt Sara John, from Dyfed-Powys Police's serious collision investigation unit, said: "The sentences passed today cannot undo the tragic loss suffered by Rhys's family."

She added she hoped the outcome "provides them with some closure as they begin to move forward with their lives, which have been changed forever".

"The actions of Abubakr and Umar Yusaf on that day were catastrophic. Their choice to drive in the manner they did shows their utter disregard towards other road users."

News.title: Police make further arrests as Thetford disorder continues
News.content:
The Labour MP for South West Norfolk, Terry Jermy, said the unrest had "put Thetford back decades" after years of trying to improve the town's reputation.

Speaking to the BBC on Friday, he said: "It's been awful the last few nights, it's been terrifying for many Thetford residents."

He said he had been made aware of properties being "pelted with eggs" on Thursday and said the town was "on edge".

He said the violence was "scaring and terrifying people who live in Thetford, particularly people from minority ethnic communities who are contacting me terrified that they are going to be misidentified as an asylum seeker and attacked".

He urged fellow politicians to "call out" the violent protests and assaults of police officers.

Jermy has previously called on the Home Office to end "secrecy and confusion" around plans to house more asylum seekers in former military barracks â including at RAF Barnham, near Thetford.

The town's mayor, Vic Peters, said he supported peaceful protests but condemned "willful disregard of the law".

Commenting as an individual and not on behalf of the town council, he said council staff had been subjected to abuse and intimidation and councillors have been verbally abused in the past week.

Scott Hussey, a Reform councillor for the nearby Brecks division on Norfolk County Council, said a "peaceful protest" had started at the town's police station on Wednesday night before it moved to Clover Way.

He described the protest as "spirited" and said there had been "some skirmishes" but said he saw no violence.

He accused the Home Office of "opening a number of these HMOs across Thetford" and "trying to rush through the site for asylum seekers at Barnham".

A Home Office spokesperson condemned the behaviour, warning that "anyone taking part in this criminal activity will face the full force of the law".

They acknowledged concerns about immigration in Thetford but condemned the violence of some protesters.

A spokesperson said: "The right to protest is fundamental to our democracy and the concerns of communities are central to our immigration reforms."

News.title: Conservatives pledge to ban foreign nationals from social housing
News.content:
The Conservatives have said they would end the provision of social housing for foreign nationals in England if they win power at the next election.

The party said ending new tenancies for all foreign nationals, as well as current tenancies for couples where neither person is a UK, Irish or EU citizen, would free up an estimated 228,144 homes for British families.

The Conservatives said Labour had "lost control of immigration" and British families had been left sitting on housing waiting lists as a result.

But Labour said the policy was an "unserious, unworkable proposal, copied from Reform, that does nothing to tackle the housing crisis the Tories themselves created".

In June, Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said he would make it a requirement for foreign national tenants to find private accommodation within three months or face possible deportation if his party won power.

Under the Tory proposals, ineligible tenants would be expected to move out of their homes within six months.

Any single person currently living in social housing who is not a UK, Irish or EU citizen would lose their social home. This includes those with or without children.

Couples, where neither of them are UK or EU citizens, and they do not have EU settled status, will also lose their entitlement.

Anyone with EU settled status would not be evicted.

For future tenancies, UK nationals and those with EU settled status would be eligible but any new EU citizens without settled status would not be.

Foreign nationals with settled status, refugee status, or specific humanitarian protections can currently qualify for social housing.

Asylum seekers are not eligible for social housing, unless in exceptional circumstances such as domestic abuse cases.

Social housing, usually provided by housing associations or local councils, is typically cheaper and more secure than privately rented homes.

When they were last in government in 2024, the Conservatives were considering plans to make it a requirement for foreign nationals to have to live in the UK for 10 years before qualifying for social housing.

There are 1.34 million households on social housing waiting lists, as of March 2025, the latest government figures.

The vast majority of social housing lettings are given to single people.

In 2024-25, most lead tenants of new social lettings, the person in whose name the social home is rented, were UK nationals - 89% or 233,000 tenants.

In the same period, 2.3% of new lettings were given to refugees - 800 refugees were UK nationals, while the remaining 3,900 were non-UK nationals.

The most common nationality of refugees in a new social letting was Afghanistan with the second most common being Ukraine.

News.title: Two firms guilty over man killed by falling window
News.content:
Two companies have been found guilty of health and safety breaches after a coach driver was killed by a falling window pane.

Mick Ferris, 53, died when glass weighing 130kg fell 300ft (90m) from a penthouse flat at The Corniche tower block on Albert Embankment in central London in October 2018.

St James Group Ltd and specialist contractors Lindner Prater Ltd were convicted at Inner London Crown Court of "failing to discharge a duty" under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. The firms will be sentenced on 24 September.

Foster + Partners, the architecture firm behind The Gherkin, and engineering consultants Wintech Ltd were cleared of the same charges.

During the trial, the court heard the "extraordinary" fact that a window panel had already fallen from the same development in August 2017, and the design was not substantially changed as a result.

Prosecuting, Gordon Menzies said: "It's reasonably practicable for clever people to do a simple thing and design a window that doesn't fall out once every year."

News.title: Girl, 11, found dead after search at Midlothian beauty spot
News.content:
An 11-year-old girl has died after being found in the water at a beauty spot in Midlothian.

A major search was launched over reports of concern for the girl in Gore Glen Woodland Park, near Gorebridge, at about 12:40 on Thursday.

The girl's body was found in the park's Gore Water, near Shank Bridge, at about 16:25. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "Her death is being treated as unexplained and inquiries are ongoing to establish the full circumstances."

The force said the girl's family was aware.

News.title: Assistant referee Massey-Ellis retires to take FA role
News.content:
Assistant referee Sian MasseyâEllis has announced her retirement from officiating to take up a position with the Football Association.

MasseyâEllis, who officiated in more than 150 Premier League matches, will start a senior manager role focused on supporting and developing female officials.

Since rising to the Premier League as an assistant referee in 2010 - becoming only the second woman to do so - MasseyâEllis became the first Englishwoman to officiate in a men's European fixture and first woman to officiate in a men's FA Cup final, as well as being involved in five Women's FA Cup finals.

After announcing her retirement, the 40-year-old said: "Although I am stepping away from the touchline, I am not stepping away from football.

"If my journey has helped change perceptions, open doors or inspire even one young person to believe they belong in the game, then I will consider that one of my greatest achievements."

News.title: London launches bid to host WorldPride in 2032
News.content:
London has launched a bid to host WorldPride 2032, which would coincide with the 60th anniversary of the UK's first Pride march in the capital in 1972.

The bid for the 10-day festival is led by Pride in London, entertainment hub Outernet London and UK Black Pride, with backing from City Hall.

Organisers have started a global campaign inviting LGBTQ+ creatives to design the official logo outline for the bid.

The winning design - which carries a Â£3,000 prize - will be filled with thousands of photographs submitted by LGBTQ+ individuals and allies worldwide, "creating one living symbol of Pride", organisers said.

Rebecca Paisis, chief executive of Pride in London, said the initiative aims to let the community shape the bid's future from day one.

"As we approach the 60th anniversary of London's first Pride march, this project gives every generation an opportunity to leave their mark on what could become one of the defining moments in our movement's history," she said.

WorldPride is a major international event featuring marches, human rights conferences and cultural festivals.

Held every two to three years, the festival aims to promote LGBTQ+ visibility and rights internationally.

Since the inaugural event in Rome in 2000, host cities have included Toronto, Madrid, New York, Copenhagen and Sydney.

London previously hosted the event in 2012 and unsuccessfully bid to stage it again in 2030, while the 2026 event is currently taking place in Amsterdam and Cape Town is set to become the first African host city in 2028.

News.title: Sullivan set to attend West Ham tie against advice
News.content:
West Ham are expecting David Sullivan to attend Saturday's Carabao Cup first-round tie against Portsmouth despite him being advised to stay away from home matches at London Stadium.

Sullivan, 77, resigned from his position as co-chair of West Ham in June after a joint investigation by BBC Panorama and The Times revealed that seven women have accused Sullivan of sexually exploitative and predatory behaviour.

He has categorically denied the allegations.

On Monday, a spokesperson for London Stadium told BBC News it had "recommended" to West Ham that Sullivan does not attend matches because of concerns about fan unrest.

London Stadium has asked for advance notice of any planned visits by major shareholder Sullivan - who retains a 38.8% stake in the club - in order to implement additional safety and operational measures.

The match against Portsmouth will be the first the club has played since the allegations against Sullivan were first reported.

The Panorama and Times joint investigation also revealed that Sullivan has been banned from contact with West Ham's women's and youth teams for the past three years because of safeguarding concerns.

London Stadium was unaware of the restrictions until the BBC's report.

Sullivan was banned after a historical allegation about his conduct was raised with the Football Association in 2023. He has previously said the allegation was false.

Sullivan had already been the subject of intense fan abuse for his running of the club, who were relegated to the Championship last season for the first time since 2011.

Although West Ham have stabilised on the pitch, with key figures, including manager Nuno Espirito Santo and skipper Jarrod Bowen committing their future to the club, there remains huge uncertainty off it.

Vanessa Gold, daughter of Sullivan's late business partner and former West Ham co-chair David, backed out of a deal to sell part of her stake in the club to Czech billionaire Daniel Kretinsky, and instead reached an agreement with Amanda Staveley, the public face of the Saudi Arabia-backed takeover at Newcastle, to sell her entire 25.1% stake.

However, Kretinsky has since sold a small part of his own stake, bringing him under 25%.

That would allow him to buy Gold's shares under West Ham's pre-emption rights rules - which allow existing shareholders first choice to buy shares when they become available.

If he did so he would become West Ham's biggest shareholder, without triggering another clause that would force him to then buy the rest of the club.

It is anticipated Saturday's match against fellow Championship side Portsmouth (15:00 BST) will set an attendance record for an EFL Cup first-round tie, with the Hammers having sold 55,000 season tickets for the new campaign.

News.content:

Iconic music producer William Orbit – who worked with the likes of Madonna, All Saints and Blur – has died at the age of 69.

In a prolific career spanning four decades, Orbit both released his own music and worked with other acts as a producer and songwriter, winning multiple Grammy Awards.

His death was announced on Friday (7 August). A post on the musician’s official Instagram account said he died at home on 23 July.

A statement, attributed to his family and friends, said: “We are deeply saddened by his passing. He will be greatly missed by us and by so many whose lives he touched with his music, friendship and kindness.”

Orbit defined the spacey sound of late Nineties and early Noughties pop, fusing electronica with jungle, trip-hop and new-age and dominating the charts with production on songs including All Saints’s “Pure Shores”, Blur’s “Coffee & TV” and several by Madonna, with whom he had his most fruitful collaboration.

After being impressed by his work on a remix of one of her early Nineties singles, Madonna personally selected Orbit to produce what would become her 1998 album Ray of Light. Widely considered one of the greatest bodies of work in her back catalogue, Ray of Light featured blockbuster singles including “Frozen”, “The Power of Good-bye” and its title track.

He’d further collaborate with her on the Austin Powers 2 single “Beautiful Stranger”, along with songs on her later albums including 2000’s Music. Other artists who went on to work with Orbit included U2, No Doubt, Melanie C, Pink and Britney Spears.

The Spice Girls’ Mel C, who tapped Orbit up for her debut solo album Northern Star in 1999, wrote on Instagram: “Such an honour to have worked with this great man. Sending all my love.”

“I remember going to William’s studio many years ago, I was so nervous but he was so warm and unassuming and genuinely curious about me and my music,” said singer Katy B. “I still remember how welcome I felt. What an amazing legacy and major loss.”

“For you, it's a joke, but for me it's not,” the frustrated mayor of a small town in northern Italy told reporters, leading a dramatic search operation like no other.

Caught in the bright flash of a local worker’s camera, a giant Papuan monitor lizard was spotted weeks ago around the Gasparina farmhouse near the town of Montichiari, in Italy’s Lombardian countryside.

First seen in early July, more than 13,000 kilometres from its native habitat of Papua New Guinea, the reptile quickly captured the country’s attention. Local authorities mobilised vast resources for the search and have banned pedestrians from walking in the area it was sighted.

But what started as a fascinating hunt for the elusive lizard, followed by a captivated social media audience, quickly turned into a headache for local authorities.

“I'm harassed all day by newspapers, media, and TV,” mayor Marco Togni told reporters according to Il Gorno Brescia. “Whoever abandoned him is an idiot, but this story must end: if it's true that he's dead, let us find him.”

open image in gallery The large reptile was first spotted ( Italian media )

Italian outlet La Sicilia said in late July there had been three sightings in just two weeks.

But in an appealing for more sightings, the mayor assured that if it is dead, whoever finds it will not be in trouble. It is illegal to either keep or kill - except in self-defence - any reptiles of the Varanidae family in Italy, including the Papuan monitor.

"If he's dead, I don't care whose fault it is, but I simply ask that he be placed on the side of a road clearly visible to everyone, so we can close this matter and leave the provincial police and forestry police free to devote themselves to other matters,” the mayor added, one fortnight after the photograph was taken.

It appears the reptile is still on the loose. The Independent has contacted the Montichiri council and Italian Cabanieri for an update but not yet received a response.

Bresciaoggi reported that authorities have used drones and cage traps in their search for the lizard. Television crews from broadcasters Rai and Mediaset have also attempted to locate the large animal.

According to The Times, thermal imagery and night vision is being used in the search for the 1.5-metre lizard. “The reptile is cold-blooded,” Togni told the outlet. “It warms itself in the sun, so we hope the thermal cameras will detect a difference in temperature.”

The Papuan monitor, also known as a crocodile monitor, is threatened by poaching and deforestation, and is protected by CITES, a multilateral treaty that protects endangered animals from the threat of international trade.

open image in gallery The crocodile monitor is threatened by poaching and deforestation ( Wiki Commons )

They typically have blunt, rounded heads with long, sharp teeth and curved claws, and can grow as big as 2.5 metres long. Living among the swamps and coastal rainforests in southeastern New Guinea, they feed on anything from small mammals, to birds, and even other smaller reptiles.

Encyclopedia Britannica lists them as the third most dangerous lizard in the world, known for being very aggressive when approached.

Togni told The Times that local authorities do not know how it ended up in northern Italy, and proposed it must have been kept illegally. “It either escaped or was abandoned.”

When he first saw the animal, he “didn’t initially believe it could be true”, but after authorities verified the image they have confirmed that it is “absolutely real”.

For the locals, the presence of the lizard in their local area presents a constant danger.

"Shortly after that famous sighting and photograph, we glimpsed the animal fleeing, let's say we saw a shadow," said the owner of the Gasparini farmhouse, where the lizard was first spotted, speaking to Bresciaoggi.

"We were afraid for our men who go out to irrigate at night, but we haven't seen it since. We don't know exactly how long it's been around or where it's hiding, but we certainly have an idea,” he added.

“Between Lonato and Calcinato, after a double bend, there are underground canals of the Medio Chiese River, disused but still with water; it could be hiding around there."

News.title: Serial sex offender guilty of murdering two women and raping a third
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A jobless serial sex offender has been found guilty of murdering two women and raping a third.

Simon Levy, 40, of Tottenham, north London, was convicted by a jury at the Old Bailey on Friday of murdering Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo, 53, and Sheryl Wilkins, 39, five months apart last year.

He was also convicted of two counts of rape and assault occasioning grievous bodily harm (GBH) with intent, as well as non-fatal suffocation over a brutal sex attack in January 2025, which the victim survived.

Prosecutor Tom Little KC told jurors the crimes were a series of attacks committed by a “predatory serial sexual attacker in a similar way”.

Miss Valencia-Trujillo was found dead in a largely abandoned block of flats on the Aylesbury Estate in south-east London on March 17 last year, while Miss Wilkins was discovered behind a car park wall on High Road, Tottenham, north London, on August 24.

open image in gallery Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo ( Metropolitan Police )

The car park was also where Levy carried out the January rape, which left the victim unconscious with a broken collarbone.

Levy was brought into police custody for questioning on September 4 and charged soon after.

Jurors heard that Levy was already a registered sex offender. He sexually assaulted two women in 2018 and was jailed in 2021.

After he was released in 2023, he carried on preying on women, and earlier this year was convicted of 11 counts of sexual assault in a separate trial at Inner London Crown Court.

open image in gallery Sheryl Wilkins ( Metropolitan Police )

Ten of the victims were young women who were using the Tube and London Overground, and the 11th was a prison officer assaulted while he was previously behind bars in 2022.

An Old Bailey jury reached verdicts after deliberating for 13 hours.

Levy, who wore sunglasses in court, made no reaction as the verdicts were delivered and members of the victims’ families wept.

At the time charges were laid, Commander Clair Kelland, who leads the Met’s Public Protection Team, said: “As the lead for public protection at the Met, one of our main priorities is to better protect women and girls.

“The investigation into Simon Levy is one of great complexity. We are working closely with partners across relevant boroughs, including Haringey and Southwark, to encourage reporting and raise awareness of the support we can provide to victim-survivors.

“Whether you are a victim-survivor, or someone with information, we urge you to come forward and speak to us.”

People can contact the Metropolitan Police’s incident room directly on 07751 700 330 or anonymously via Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Police find two bodies buried in backyard after relatives request wellness check
News.content:
Police have launched an international manhunt for Matthew Flores, 27, after two bodies were discovered buried in the backyard of a home in Lichfield Park, Arizona.

The grim discovery was made on Thursday after relatives requested a welfare check on the couple living at the property and their adult son, Matthew Flores, on Tuesday.

A missing person’s investigation was commenced in response to the “suspicious circumstances” of the trio’s disappearance, with the Avondale Police Department notifying local residents via a Facebook video message in which it appealed for information but said there was no threat posted to the wider community.

The Avondale Police Department has not named the victims but is seeking Matthew Flores, who is believed to have fled the country and is considered a suspect in the missing persons case.

Neighbors expressed shock at the incident in their quiet area, with some reporting hearing yelling from the property prior to the welfare check.

The long-awaited, well-deserved holiday season has finally arrived for millions of employees. However, after months of non-stop work, truly unplugging can become incredibly difficult. Modern workplaces demand a state of constant mental availability. Driven by rapid technological advances, we find ourselves endlessly tied to work through group chats, social media, and e-mails, making total disconnection a challenge. This technological complexity is also associated with greater emotional exhaustion at work and in our personal lives.

Along with daily and weekly breaks between shifts, annual leave periods are designed to be one of the most effective tools for essential rest and recovery.

Research consistently shows that time away from work can improve wellbeing, reduce exhaustion and support recovery. It actively lowers stress, improves sleep quality, and reduces the risk of chronic illness. The stakes are incredibly high: according to estimates by the International Labour Organization, over 840,000 people die annually from health conditions tied to psychosocial risks, including, among other, long working hours, excessive demands, and poor shift scheduling.

open image in gallery Along with daily and weekly breaks between shifts, annual leave periods are designed to be one of the most effective tools for essential rest and recovery ( Getty/iStock )

The elusive work-life balance

Switching off from work is not easy, and a change of location is often not enough. Whether we travel or remain at home, unfinished tasks can continue to occupy our attention. We may feel anxious about what has been left open or compelled to finish everything before leaving. These experiences form part of an ongoing research project at the University of Zurich’s Center for Leadership in the Future of Work into how perceptions of time, unfinished work and feelings of urgency shape people’s experiences in organisations.

Psychologists describe part of this impulse as the desire for closure: the motivation to complete a goal for the sake of resolving it, even when finishing immediately carries additional costs. Completing our goals is satisfying and feels good. Unfinished goals, by contrast, can interfere with other aspects of our work and life by creating intrusive thoughts during unrelated tasks.

A recent study showed that people have a stronger desire for closure before a vacation (compared to a normal workday). Specifically, people showed more impatience to finish off tasks before taking holidays, even without a pressing deadline, and even when that meant working overtime. The logic is simple: we don’t want to think about work during our time off.

Naturally, this poses a challenge for those of us who anticipate a post-vacation workload, as vacations may prove less restful than expected if a backlog of tasks awaits in our inbox. These unresolved demands can make it harder to disconnect and weaken the restorative benefits of time off.

This is not solely a matter of individual self-discipline. Employees may struggle to detach because workloads, communication norms and inadequate vacation cover make disconnection unrealistic. Employers therefore shape whether leave is genuinely restorative: they can arrange cover, redistribute urgent work, clarify that messages do not require a response and avoid allowing large backlogs to build while someone is away.

So, for holiday periods to be truly restful and restorative, both the departure and the return need to be considered. And both employees and employers can help.

How to make your time off truly restful

Before your holiday

In the days before leave, distinguish between tasks that genuinely need to be completed and those that can safely wait. For unfinished work, write down the next action, who is responsible and when you will return to it. A clear handover and restart plan can provide a sense of closure without requiring you to finish everything.

Managers can help by agreeing priorities in advance, arranging cover and avoiding unnecessary deadlines immediately before or after an employee’s leave.

During your holiday

Longer vacations can produce greater improvements in wellbeing, but duration is not the only factor that matters. A 2025 meta-analysis found that psychological detachment from work and physical activity during leave was particularly beneficial.

Activities that produce relaxation, pleasure, control and psychological detachment are especially helpful.

Timing also plays a role. The period immediately before a vacation may actually be stressful. Wellbeing can decline as holidays approach, largely due to high pre-leave workloads. However, once the holiday time starts, wellbeing tends to improve again, with studies suggesting it peaks around the eighth day.

About the author Maria Diaz-Macias is a PhD Researcher at the Center for Leadership in the Future of Work (University of Zurich), University of Zurich. Francisco Diaz Bretones is a Professor of Occupational Psychology. Dean of the Faculty of Labour Relations and Human Resources, Universidad de Granada. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article .

After your holiday

Despite the clear benefits of taking time off, returning to work can sometimes trigger a negative downturn known as the post-holiday blues: the experience of vague anxiety, increased irritability, feelings of nostalgia, sleep disturbances, and a general sense of discomfort once the summer holidays are over. To ease the transition, a few practical strategies can help employees:

Head back home one or two days before your first day of work to settle in.

Approach your work tasks gently during the first few days back. If possible, keep the first morning free of non-essential meetings.

Handle problems step-by-step, setting realistic deadlines and expectations for yourself. Prioritise the most important to-dos rather than attempting to clear the entire inbox immediately.

Ultimately, recovery depends on whether people are genuinely able to switch off from work, and whether they can return without being punished by an unmanageable backlog. Employees can create clearer boundaries and plans, but employers must design workloads and communication practices that make switching off possible in the first place.

News.title: Gomes scores for Aston Villa in defeat by Bayern Munich in Hong Kong
News.content:
Aston Villa 1 Bayern Munich 2

Aston Villa’s tour of the Far East ended in defeat as they lost 2-1 to German champions Bayern Munich in a pre-season friendly at the Kai Tak Sports Park in Hong Kong on Friday.

Bayern took the lead inside the final 10 minutes of the first half, with defender Kim Min-jae heading in from Tom Bischof’s sublime free-kick. Villa goalkeeper Marco Bizot made a string of saves in the second half to keep Bayern’s lead at one goal until former Liverpool forward Luis Díaz smashed in Bayern’s second off the underside of the bar.

Just as the game appeared to be out of reach for Aston Villa, who had struggled to create much going forward for most of the game, Unai Emery’s side showed some life late on. Summer signing João Gomes’s goal from the edge of the box gave them hope before Tammy Abraham nearly brought them back onto level terms, only to be denied by a fine save from 40-year-old Manuel Neuer.

Aston Villa are next in action in six days’ time when they take on Paris St-Germain in the Uefa Super Cup before kicking off their Premier League campaign at Brighton. Bayern have one more friendly to come against RB Leipzig before the DFL-Supercup against Borussia Dortmund. They then kick off the defence of their Bundesliga crown against Stuttgart at home on August 28.

News.title: Suspected Ebola case on packed Congo river boat sparks testing rush
News.content:
Congolese health authorities have intercepted and detained a river boat on its way to the capital after a suspected Ebola case onboard.

Authorities have set up a mobile clinic to test more than 200 passengers after one of them disembarked and died earlier on the voyage.

The boat travelling from the northeastern commercial hub of Kisangani was stopped and held in Maluku, some 40 miles from Kinshasa.

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is dealing with its worst ever outbreak of the viral haemorrhagic fever, which has seen nearly 4,000 cases and killed around 1,801 people according to the latest government figures.

Samuel Roger Kamba, the health minister, said a 32-year-old man had disembarked in Pimu in Mongala province, before developing ‌suspected Ebola symptoms and dying.

“We did not say it was Ebola. We said there was a suspected case for which we are being cautious,” the health minister told a press conference, according to MediaCongo, a local news site.

He said there had been no other reports of deaths among travellers.

The virus has so far spread to five provinces, though more than 90 per cent of cases have been recorded in the north eastern Ituri region.

News.content:
From gracious old farmsteads and magnificent manor houses to an ancient coaching inn creaking with Tudor character, the top luxury hotels in the Cotswolds combine a wonderful sense of history with contemporary style and outstanding modern British cuisine. They all excel in providing creature comforts, whether crackling fires by kick-back sofas, canopy beds with soft throws, or suites with terraces and hot tubs.
