World.title: Kalshi and Polymarket bets on clinical trials criticized as 'ghastly'
World.content:
Kalshi and Polymarket bets on clinical trials criticized as 'ghastly'

toggle caption Fred Tanneau/AFP via Getty Images

As a soon-to-be seventh grader, Joshua Pederson's son is not exactly brimming with enthusiasm when he talks about the upcoming school year.

"The thing I'm looking forward to most in seventh grade is lunch, and the thing I'm looking forward to least is everything else," said the 12-year-old.

Art is his passion, but he doesn't take classes. He likes teaching himself.

"I like drawing scary stuff and robots," he said. "Because I think scary stuff and robots are cool."

Two years ago, his parents, who live in Boston, noticed a lump around his ribs that quickly spiraled into a nightmare scenario: It was cancer.

Pederson asked that his son's name be withheld to discuss details of his medical condition.

After months of grueling chemotherapy and radiation, he was declared cancer-free last summer. Months later, however, the cancer returned. So Pederson entered his son into a clinical trial for a novel treatment.

Sponsor Message

That's around the time Pederson read the news that prediction market sites Kalshi and Polymarket have begun allowing people to bet on the outcomes of clinical trials and whether the Food and Drug Administration will approve new medications.

"What seemed to be missed in the CEO statements was the fact that there were going to be patients on the other side of these bets," said Pederson, who is a humanities professor at Boston University.

Bettors will make or lose money based on the success or failure of a clinical trial, a situation Pederson views as horrific.

"A clinical trial failing is a more sanitized euphemism for, people are going to suffer, people are going to die, people are going to have one fewer clinical option available to them in one of the most difficult medical situations of their entire life," he said.

Researchers fear 'undermining trial integrity'

Billions of dollars are traded every week on the lightly regulated prediction market sites, where users bet on everything from movie reviews to elections to conflicts in the Middle East. Clinical trials are just the latest area where the industry's rapid growth is raising ethical questions.

Kalshi claims such bets will provide a new source of information about which drugs will get approved, and what clinical trials will show promising results, which the company says can help investors decide what new drugs to fund.

Sponsor Message

"If you want to ban profiting from the failure of clinical trials, you would start with the stock market, where the financial incentive for this type of profit is orders of magnitude larger," said Kalshi spokesman Jack Such, pointing to stock market short sellers who have profited from clinical trial failures.

"While Kalshi and the stock market are the same in this regard, they do differ in one important way: the stock market doesn't give any valuable information to researchers," Such said.

Drug trial researchers, though, are far from convinced.

David Tsai, who runs clinical trials at a biotech company in the San Francisco Bay Area, started an online petition pushing for such betting to be banned, making the case that betting on drug trials "threatens the very foundation of trust and integrity in biotechnology."

Tsai is concerned that the prospect of betting provides those involved with a clinical trial a reason to tamper with the results for a prediction market payout.

"If we were running a trial for an oncology drug that requires an infusion, a pharmacist who had placed a bet saying that it's gonna work well, or doesn't work well, could obviously adjust the infusion rate, could adjust the source temperature of the drug," he said. "They could change any number of variables that could obviously have a direct impact [on] how the trial and the data and the patient safety would come out."

Another skeptic is Nicholas Zaorsky, a professor of radiation oncology at the Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Fla., who has helped run clinical trials and agrees that prediction markets can interfere with the advancement of life-saving drugs.

"Prediction markets can be valuable in some settings because they aggregate information, but clinical trials are fundamentally different: investigators, coordinators, and sometimes even participants can directly influence aspects of the outcomes being wagered on," Zaorsky said. "That creates financial incentives that risk undermining trial integrity."

Sponsor Message

Patient's father: People betting on trials are 'distanced from the real cost'

Kalshi has tapped its own experts, including Anne Wojcicki, the founder of genetic testing company 23andMe, to vouch for the markets as a way of staying ahead of medical breakthroughs and for making clinical trials more accessible.

"Most patients don't know about the choices available in clinical trials or which programs are most promising. The opportunity to have an open, transparent dataset about trial probabilities is extremely promising and empowering for people," a white paper sponsored by Kalshi stated.

On Kalshi, users can currently bet on whether a weight-loss medication and a breast cancer treatment will be approved by federal regulators and on what date.

Polymarket, which declined to comment, is taking wagers on the approval of cancer treatments and whether the U.S. will allow Chinese peptides to be sold to Americans.

The possibility of insider trading, Kalshi argues, will be minimized by company safeguards verifying employment and tools to surveil for unusual market activity.

Indeed, prediction markets have helped identify insider traders in other markets, from President Trump's teleprompter operator to former Congressman George Santos to a special forces soldier who was betting based on military intelligence about the toppling of Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro.

Given just how many people can be involved with clinical trials, Tsai thinks it might not be so easy to preemptively catch every bad actor.

Pederson is also skeptical. He argues the markets obscure the patients at the center of clinical trials, who have the most at stake from their outcomes.

"One of the things that has struck me about these platforms is that they're flashy and they're gamified in such a way that you're often kind of distanced from the real cost," he said.

Kalshi says it is offering bets on late-stage clinical trials where participants have already been chosen. And it says it won't allow betting on markets where all trial subjects are minors. But that could change.

Sponsor Message

If it does, Pederson says wondering whether researchers in a trial could be motivated by prediction market profits will add to his anxieties — and to the burden his son is already carrying.

"The weight on him and what he's being asked to do, and what he's being asked to endure, is already so much," Pederson said.

He hopes that Kalshi and Polymarket will stop letting speculators place bets that clinical trials won't succeed.

Bettors, he argues, should not be rooting for an experimental medicine to fail just to earn a buck.

"It's a dark idea," he said. "It's quite ghastly."

World.title: Everyone's talking about hormone therapy for menopause. Should I be on it?
World.content:
Everyone's talking about hormone therapy for menopause. Should I be on it?

Sunnu Rebecca Choi for NPR

Dr. Mara Gordon, a family physician in Camden, N.J., answers reader health questions monthly. Send in your question to: thrive@npr.org.

Q: I am in perimenopause. I keep seeing posts all over social media talking up menopausal hormone therapy as a cure-all. Should I be taking hormones? Should everyone?

A: I'm not surprised that you've been hearing the hype. There's been an explosion of menopause content from influencers, direct-to-consumer telehealth companies marketing to women in midlife, and new books and podcasts on the topic.

Sponsor Message

This is great news for women. Menopause has historically been under-studied and stigmatized, so I love seeing more open conversations about this stage of life. And the pendulum has swung on hormone therapy; medical groups now recommend it again for many patients, after years of cautioning against it.

It's about time that women have access to treatments for the very real symptoms that can accompany menopause, rather than being told to "deal with" their hot flashes or sleep disruption.

But I'm also seeing a lot of less-than-scientific misinformation out there that over-promises on what menopausal hormone therapy can do. There are also lots of less-than-ethical influencers who are looking to make a quick buck on unproven supplements and vitamins.

As I navigate the new focus on menopause care alongside my patients, I've realized how critical it is to separate the hype from the reality.

Here's what the science says about menopausal hormone therapy — and what we don't yet know.

For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

What we mean when we say hormone therapy

Two types of hormones tend to decline in female bodies as we age: estrogen and progesterone.

When doctors prescribe menopausal hormone therapy, it's typically either estrogen alone or estrogen plus a progestogen, a term that includes the progesterone naturally found in the body and the synthetic hormones that mimic it.

Sponsor Message

These medications come in many different formulations, including transdermal patches, pills, and vaginal creams and rings.

You can get systemic hormone therapy — that's hormones that are absorbed throughout the body — or local therapy, like a vaginal estrogen that only affects the vulva. These treatments have different risks and benefits, and you might need different combinations of them depending on your symptoms.

Some doctors use testosterone to treat sexual dysfunction in women, but doctors generally don't use the term menopausal hormone therapy when they're talking about testosterone.

Why the pendulum has swung on hormone therapy

When I was in medical school in the 2010s, I learned that hormone therapy could be dangerous.

The idea came from the Women's Health Initiative that followed thousands of women in midlife who were taking hormones throughout the 1990s and early 2000s. Researchers actually stopped it early because it seemed to show that hormone therapy increased the risk of heart disease, breast cancer, stroke and pulmonary embolism.

After this news, prescriptions for hormone therapy went down dramatically. In 1999-2000, 22% of American women over 40 were receiving menopausal hormone therapy, one study estimated. By 2010, researchers estimated that had dropped to just around 5% of women in that age group.

But then, researchers began to reanalyze data from the Women's Health Initiative. The growing consensus is that menopausal hormone therapy is much safer than we thought for women in their late 40s and 50s.

Once that news started to spread — and go viral online — patient demand began to spike.

What symptoms are the hormones good at treating?

The primary reason doctors recommend systemic hormone therapy is to treat what are called vasomotor symptoms of menopause, otherwise known as "hot flashes."

Some researchers estimate that up to 80% of women in the menopausal transition have hot flashes — and they can really affect women's quality of life. Some of my patients tell me that they disrupt their sleep, their ability to focus at work, and sometimes feel so distracting that they don't want to leave the house.

Sponsor Message

Systemic hormone therapy can help prevent fractures for those at high risk of osteoporosis. It also helps keep bones strong as women age, although most organizations don't recommend it to be used only for this purpose. I think of bone loss prevention as a positive side effect of hormone therapy when I prescribe it for hot flashes, but it's not clear that the benefits outweigh the risks for every single patient.

Hormone therapy is also used to treat premature menopause if a woman has had her ovaries removed.

Dryness and irritation in the vulva — known as the genitourinary syndrome of menopause — also often get better with hormone therapy. These symptoms often improve with an estrogen treatment in the vagina, such as a cream or a ring; systemic hormone therapy can help too.

And should I take them for heart health and longevity benefits?

Hormone therapy can be life-changing for women experiencing hot flashes. But it's not the fountain of youth, as many influencers seem to promise.

Most major medical organizations — including the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, and the Menopause Society — do not recommend hormone therapy for longevity, heart health, or preventing chronic conditions, based on the data currently available. (It's not recommended for youthful-looking skin and hair, another overly optimistic claim I've seen online!)

Still, there's some genuine uncertainty about whether hormone therapy might help prevent heart disease.

"It's really an unanswered question right now," said Dr. Karen Adams, a professor of obstetrics and gynecology at Stanford, where she directs the Program in Menopause and Healthy Aging.

Adams says there is promising research that suggests that hormone therapy, when taken before age 60 or within 10 years since menopause, might help prevent atherosclerosis, heart attacks and strokes. But other studies show that hormone therapy — particularly when taken over age 60 — has no cardiovascular benefit at all or may even increase heart disease risk.

Sponsor Message

Essentially, researchers say that using hormone therapy right around the menopausal transition, usually in a woman's early 50s, seems to be much safer than using it later in life.

The way that women take hormones seems to matter, too. Research generally shows that transdermal estrogen — delivered through a patch — is less likely to cause blood clots than oral estrogen.

So for patients in their late 40s and 50s with hot flashes or night sweats, Adams liberally prescribes hormone therapy unless patients have a clear medical reason not to. (More on that below!) But when it comes to heart health, she tends to focus on other prevention tools, like blood pressure management, cholesterol medications, nutrition and exercise.

"I don't say, 'Here, take hormone therapy. It's going to keep you from having a heart attack,'" Adams said. "We don't have that data. And I don't make that promise."

Who should not take hormones

There are definitely reasons to proceed with caution when it comes to menopausal hormone therapy.

Anyone who has had breast cancer, blood clots, or a heart attack or stroke should have an in-depth conversation with their doctor about it, because hormone therapy can make those conditions worse or increase the risk of them recurring.

If I saw a patient with one of those conditions who was experiencing hot flashes, I'd probably recommend they try a nonhormonal treatment option first. Certain types of antidepressants can reduce hot flash frequency and severity. If the antidepressants aren't effective, women have several other options, including a medication called fezolinetant, which was approved by the Food and Drug Administration in 2023.

To help prevent loss of bone density in a patient who can't take hormones, I'd recommend that old standby: exercise. Weight-bearing exercise is one of the most effective tools we have to help prevent osteoporosis.

Sponsor Message

A family history of breast cancer doesn't mean a patient can't consider hormone therapy. But it's important to proceed with caution. In that scenario, I'd first do a formal breast cancer risk assessment and think about genetic testing for high-risk mutations.

If the patient really wanted to use hormone therapy, I'd recommend what professional prescribing guidelines suggest: Take the minimum dose of hormone therapy that effectively treats your symptoms for the shortest possible duration.

Ultimately, it's about understanding your own values and preferences.

"I lay out the risks and benefits," said Dr. Jessica Platt, a family physician in Massachusetts who focuses on women's health and menopause care. "Giving people knowledge and also giving them patient autonomy."

The bottom line

Just because menopause hormone therapy is much safer than doctors believed in the 2000s doesn't mean it's a cure-all. Adams is concerned that some women might end up using a treatment that does more harm than good.

"When we just say this is the fountain of youth, people believe that. And women can be harmed by that," Adams said.

In my own practice, I've come to realize there's no one-size-fits-all answer.

Hormone therapy can really improve my patients' quality of life. It's gratifying when a patient comes to see me and says, "Thank you! My hot flashes are finally under control!"

But hormone therapy, unfortunately, does not fix every ailment the online influencers promise it will. It's not right for everyone.

Ultimately, the decision to use hormone therapy should be a discussion between doctor and patient that takes into account the patient's medical history, symptoms and values.

Dr. Mara Gordon is a family physician in Camden, N.J. She writes the newsletter Your Doctor Friend.

World.title: Amid cost of living stress, many parents are supporting children well into adulthood
World.content:
Amid cost of living stress, many parents are supporting children well into adulthood

toggle caption Mabel Lago

Mabel Lago and her husband are retired and in their 70s. But before they decided to move from New Jersey to South Carolina this year, they checked with their younger son. That's because he was still living with them, at age 39.

"We could not leave him behind, because he could not afford to live on his own," she said.

Her son is a hard worker, she explains, but his job helping to manage a liquor store paid low wages and no benefits. He also has Type 1 diabetes, and his Affordable Care Act insurance was nearly a thousand dollars a month. So he came with them to South Carolina, where his plan now is a lot cheaper — but he hasn't yet landed a new job.

Sponsor Message

"The young people have really been shafted, big time, with the economy, with the cost of living," Lago said.

She is among a majority of Americans who, according to polls, think it's more difficult for young adults today to achieve financial independence than it was for their parents. It's a view that's grown sharply in recent years, as prices for essentials such as housing, food and energy have shot up and inflation has stayed stubbornly elevated.

Such concerns partly explain why most parents help support their grown children in some way, many well beyond the traditional age of financial independence. The share of 25- to 34-year-olds living with parents has also nearly doubled since 2005, to about 20%, according to the Urban Institute. One analysis found a third of all those under 35 are living back at home, just shy of the record peak during the COVID-19 pandemic, even though most are employed.

Lago and her husband built their 1,500-square-foot retirement home in South Carolina a bit larger than they might have, to include a bedroom for their son. They also gave part of the land they bought to their older son, 43, who has a well-paying job but has not been able to buy a house on his single income. But he just built one next door, with money his parents gave him from their own inheritance.

Sponsor Message

toggle caption Mabel Lago

Lago is happy to help, but she and her husband have to watch their spending carefully. This year, as gas and food prices spiked, they cut back on driving and stopped eating beef. Now, they're thinking not only of their own long-term finances, but also that of their sons.

"Did we plan for that when we had our children 40 years ago? No," she said. "Do we plan for that now? Yes, we have to."

"A different economic landscape"

Some parents have long helped children — pitching in so they can buy a first home, for example. But over recent decades, as families have gotten smaller and people marry later, researchers have found more parents have done so and in larger amounts.

"Young adults are kind of coming of age in a different economic landscape than their parents did," said Rachel Minkin, a researcher at the Pew Research Center.

A Pew survey this year found a growing majority of Americans say it's harder today for young people to find a job, pay for college, buy a home and save for the future. In a new survey question, 80% even agreed that "it's harder for young adults today to cover basic expenses," Minkin said.

A 2024 Pew analysis found young adults are also more likely to have student loan debt compared to three decades ago. And while the share with mortgage debt was about the same, the median amount of that debt adjusted for inflation was larger.

This changing economic landscape has helped fuel the rise in adult children living with parents.

An AARP survey last year found 75% of parents across income levels help support adult children in some way, from paying cellphone and Wi-Fi fees, to helping with transportation and rent, or giving straight cash. On average, that amounts to $7,000 a year.

"What's striking is that so many of the people we see in our survey actually were living independently for a while and then went back in with their parents, primarily because of financial pressures," said Richard Johnson, who leads a financial security policy team at AARP.

Most give because they want to, not because children need it, according to the survey. But many lower-income families said they help even though it hurts their own finances.

Sponsor Message

"When people have to divert what little resources they have to help their children, and they can't put it toward retirement, that jeopardizes their own financial futures," Johnson said.

Advising parents to protect their own retirement

Nate Kinzinger, a wealth manager affiliated with the financial services firm Northwestern Mutual, has seen this shift during his 25-year career. He's had clients delay retirement in part to continue supporting adult children. So many have stepped in to pay student loan debt that he now advises families to consider the "return on investment" from a given field of study.

Clients also help with down payments or high rent, especially when children live in big cities where the cost of living can far exceed early-career wages. Others pay a monthly stipend.

"There's usually some degree of guilt, you know, and there's some degree of, well, the money's in my account, so I can do it,'" he said.

Some continue regular payments even after retirement, he said, not understanding they will need that money later. "And so we'll have to have those conversations of, all right, how do we close this gap for you, cause I'm not comfortable that you could continue doing this," Kinzinger said.

This year, Northwestern Mutual found in its own survey that 42% of Americans still feel financially dependent on their parents. That included a third of Gen Xers, who are now middle-aged.

"That was a bit of a shocking number," he said. The survey did not delve into the reasons why, but that cohort includes many of the parents helping struggling young adult children.

toggle caption David Zucchero

Is it coddling or the new norm?

David Zucchero and his wife are retired, living near Seattle, and have children ages 31, 32 and 34. Helping them out is "just an ongoing thing for all three kids," he said, and it's "gotten worse in the last, I'd say, five to eight years."

To be clear, he's well-off and all the children — or a spouse — make good pay. Over the years, the parents have helped with education and handed down old cars.

But Seattle area home prices are double the national median. A year ago, one daughter moved back home, with her husband and now two young kids, so she could be a stay-at-home mom. Another daughter wants to rent out her condo and move back home to cut down on expenses. And their son and his family? They live with his wife's parents.

Sponsor Message

"When I look at the salaries these kids make, I'm like, 'how can you not live on this?'" Zucchero said. "But they can't."

toggle caption David Zucchero

At least not comfortably, he added, admitting that he and his wife are guilty of coddling them. Zucchero's best friend chides him about it. But everyone else seems to be in the same boat.

"One or two of the kids are living at home," he said. "Neighbors, same thing, one right behind us. The kid's been living there probably 10 years, he's in his 40s."

For now, he and his wife are not charging rent or setting deadlines for anyone to move out. The truth is, they love having the children and grandkids around.

World.title: Besieged Sudanese city faces relentless drone strikes and risk of mass atrocities, U.N. warns
World.content:
Besieged Sudanese city faces relentless drone strikes and risk of mass atrocities, U.N. warns

toggle caption AFP via Getty Images/AFP

Whenever residents of the besieged city of el-Obeid look up at the sky, it is filled with drones — sometimes as many as 40 at a time.

The hum of the unmanned aircraft, which have been conducting deadly strikes on the city for months, has become the soundtrack to their days.

And the drones are indiscriminate.

"You might get hit and killed by a drone while you're asleep at home, or while on the way to school. You could also get hit by a drone in the market," says one 25-year-old resident.

The local aid worker doesn't want to be named because of the risk to her safety, but she says they even hit funerals.

Sponsor Message

Her uncle was killed in a drone strike while going to bury his neighbor — who'd been killed in a drone strike.

Sudan has been mired in a brutal civil between government forces and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) for more than three years. The war has caused the world's largest humanitarian crisis and displaced millions of people.

El-Obeid, the capital of North Kordofan state, sits along a strategic corridor in central Sudan, south of the capital, Khartoum, and on the route to the country's western Darfur region. Its location has made it a critical battleground in the war.

According to data from the International NGO Safety Organisation, North Kordofan has recorded the highest number of drone attacks in Sudan in 2026. Drones have been used by both sides to the conflict.

United Nations experts are now warning of a new risk of large-scale atrocities in el-Obeid, which they say could see a repeat of what happened in the Darfur city of el-Fasher last year, when the RSF slaughtered some 6,000 civilians. U.N. investigators later declared those crimes bore "the hallmarks of genocide."

toggle caption Satellite image ©2026 Vantor

toggle caption Satellite image ©2026 Vantor

'Red alert'

Volker Türk, the U.N. high commissioner for human rights, has stressed the need for urgent action.

Sponsor Message

"This is not a drill. It is a red alert that needs to land on the desks of heads of state and government around the world," he said last month. "Their phones should be running hot in the coming days and weeks, with ideas on how to prevent atrocity crimes in el-Obeid and in other places in Kordofan."

Already in el-Obeid, a city of about 500,000 people, the RSF is replicating tactics it used in el-Fasher, attacking critical infrastructure, including water distribution points, and causing severe water shortages.

That has left women facing a "deadly gamble" as they go out to collect water, according to U.N. Women East Africa Director Anna Mutavati.

"Under the perception that darkness offers protection from aerial attacks, these women and girls have been harassed, raped and subjected to other forms of sexual violence — all while trying to access water," she said.

Meanwhile, a deadly cholera outbreak is spreading in parts of the city, with children the worst affected.

"Cholera is tearing through certain communities in the city, with the outbreak being compounded by incessant rains and recent drone strikes that have crippled critical medical facilities and left thousands without access to urgent treatment and life-saving medications," Plan International Sudan Director Mohamed Kamal said this week.

"The situation facing children is particularly dangerous," he said. "They are far more susceptible to disease, some face the prospect of recruitment by armed groups, and they are experiencing lasting psychological trauma."

toggle caption AFP via Getty Images/AFP

U.S. senators urge action

Since the war broke out in 2023, at least 59,000 people have been killed, according to the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project, a conflict-monitoring group. But the true toll could be much higher.

Sudan's government forces have been buoyed by recent gains against the RSF. Last week, they celebrated retaking a major highway in North Kordofan and several other key positions.

Sponsor Message

But despite those military advances, Sudan researcher Eric Reeves told NPR this week: "There is no likelihood of a military rescue of el-Obeid."

More than 100,000 displaced people there are now sheltering in camps, and some are facing extreme hunger.

"Many families are struggling to meet their basic needs in IDP camps," Esperanza Santos, Sudan emergency coordinator for Doctors Without Borders, told NPR.

Aid funding cuts and rising diesel and fertilizer costs linked to the broader disruption caused by the war in Iran are also worsening the situation, according to the World Food Programme, which is distributing food in the city.

"At a time when needs continue to grow, humanitarian resources are shrinking," Derk Segaar, special Sudan envoy for the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, told a U.N. briefing in Geneva this week.

Pressure is mounting on the international community to act. On Tuesday, a group of more than 20 U.S. senators wrote to Secretary of State Marco Rubio urging him to take steps to prevent mass atrocities in el-Obeid.

"While we welcome the State Department's expression of concern about the escalating situation in el-Obeid, words are not enough," the letter, signed by Democratic Sens. Tim Kaine, Bernie Sanders and Adam Schiff, said.

"The encirclement and systematic crippling of resources in el-Obeid increasingly parallels el-Fasher," the letter continued.

The senators also urged the administration to stop selling arms to the United Arab Emirates, which has been accused of supporting the RSF.

Reeves agreed that such action from the U.S. is critical.

"Until the United Arab Emirates is called out and dissuaded from pursuing its grotesquely destructive policy in Sudan," he told NPR, "we're going to see this war continue."

World.title: Canada adds 75,000 new jobs in July, unemployment rate lowest in 2 years
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada added 75,000 jobs in July, up 0.4 per cent, as the unemployment fell to 6.4 per cent, its lowest level in two years.

Statistics Canada's labour force survey released on Friday said most of those gains were split between full- and part-time work, as wholesale and retail trade alone added 21,000 new jobs.

The agency says employment rose for people aged 25 to 54, and mostly for women in that age group.

The unemployment rate held steady at 5.8 per cent for men aged 25 to 54, StatsCan says, while falling 5.2 per cent for women in that cohort.

Ontario added the most jobs of any province in July, with 52,000, or an increase of 0.6 per cent, mostly in the professional, scientific and technical services sector. British Columbia had a similar increase, with 18,000 new jobs.

Manitoba's employment rate rose 0.8 per cent, adding 5,900 new jobs, while Nova Scotia's increased 0.8 per cent, thanks to 4,600 jobs.

Statistics Canada said the country is up 181,000 jobs since April, and 196,000 from a year ago.

Economists have previously said the labour market appeared to be stabilizing after the first quarter of the year brought a mild contraction and employers shed jobs.

The economy likely fared a lot better in the second quarter, with StatsCan estimating real GDP grew 3.4 per cent on an annualized basis over the three-month period.

However, U.S. President Donald Trump's latest threats of 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of Canadian imports are casting fresh uncertainty over employers.

World.title: Ontario Conservative MP Larry Brock to exit Parliament in September
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative MP Larry Brock says he'll be resigning from the House of Commons next month.

Brock, the MP for the Ontario riding of Brantford—Brant South—Six Nations, was elected to Parliament in two consecutive elections — first in 2021, and again in 2025.

He served as an assistant Crown attorney prior to being elected to the House of Commons.

In a letter posted to social media on Thursday, Brock said he'd "accepted an opportunity to return directly to the frontlines of justice at the Brantford Crown Attorney's office."

His resignation will take effect on Sept. 18, according to the letter announcing his exit.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre posted a brief message on X, thanking Brock for his work as an MP.

" My ardent wish is for you and your family to have all the success and happiness in the world. God bless, my friend ," Poilievre said in his post.

The Conservatives won the second-most seats in the 2025 federal election, but the party has seen seven MPs — Brock included — leave its federal caucus since that time.

Four MPs from the Conservative benches crossed the floor to join the governing Liberals — Chris d'Entremont, Michael Ma, Matt Jeneroux and Marilyn Gladu.

Richard Martel, the now-former MP for the Quebec riding of Chicoutimi—Le Fjord, was appointed to the Senate by Prime Minister Mark Carney in July.

Cathay Wagantall, a Conservative MP since 2015, is resigning her seat of Yorkton—Melville in Saskatchewan effective Aug. 31.

World.title: Canadians' climate change concerns rebound amid wildfire season
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The percentage of Canadians who see addressing climate change as a top priority spiked this summer after years of it taking a back seat to other issues, recent polling has found.

Data published by the Angus Reid Institute shows a surge in Canadians indicating climate change is one of their top concerns. In the survey where respondents were asked to choose up to three issues they care about most, 21 per cent chose the environment and climate change in July, a 50 per cent increase from March.

Angus Reid found 25 per cent of Canadians aged 18 to 34, 23 per cent aged 35 to 55 and 16 per cent older than 55 put the issue as a top concern.

Shachi Kurl, president of the Angus Reid Institute, said a higher interest in climate change among younger Canadians is "along the lines of what we've seen in the past."

Kurl said the bigger takeaway from the newest results is the consistent increase in concern across all age groups.

Angus Reid surveyed a random sample of 1,770 Canadian adults from July 25 to July 27. It said a margin of error from a probability sample of the same size would be two percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Recent polling from Abacus Data found similar results, with 18 per cent of their sample selecting environment and climate change as a top concern, an increase of three points over two weeks. Abacus asked respondents to choose three top issues from a longer list of other issues.

Abacus Data CEO David Coletto said the increase is a "notable move up" for the climate change issue.

"This is competing with issues like [U.S. President Donald] Trump and cost of living and health care," Coletto said. "It's signalling that the salience of this issue, the attention people are paying to it, is rising."

Abacus surveyed a random sample of 1,910 Canadian adults from July 23 to July 29 and said a margin of error for a comparable sample would be 2.24 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Backdrop of fires and heat waves

As Abacus and Angus Reid polled Canadians in July, wildfires raged across the country, forcing thousands to evacuate their homes. Many fires are still burning, notably in British Columbia and northwestern Ontario.

Coletto said the presence of wildfires in the news, their direct effects like smoke and global extreme weather events, like major fires in Europe, come together to "raise [climate change and the environment] back up onto the agenda."

Still, Kurl said it is yet to be seen whether this is a "more permanent uptick" when wildfires are less top of mind for Canadians.

A moment or a movement?

Even as Angus Reid recorded a 50 per cent increase between March and July, climate change and the environment is still far from its peak in voter concern at the end of the last decade.

"Climate change was the number-one issue," Kurl said. "It was arguably the ballot issue in the 2019 election, among other issues."

Forty per cent of respondents listed climate change and the environment as one of their top issues in Angus Reid's June 2019 polling.

Kurl said during the COVID-19 pandemic, climate change took "a significant back seat" to other issues quarter after quarter.

By the 2021 federal election, a focus on climate was seen in policy proposals from all parties, with the Conservative platform including a consumer carbon price, an industrial price, a zero-emission vehicle mandate and a low-carbon fuel standard.

In 2025, Prime Minister Mark Carney ended the consumer carbon tax in his first move at Canada's helm. During the 2025 election, environmental issues fell out of the top five concerns , according to data from Vote Compass .

In a "forward guidance" video released in June, Carney acknowledged that Canada's emissions would be on the rise.

"The changes we have made will mean that our emissions will be higher in the next few years than they were projected to be under the previous government's plan," Carney said.

Kurl said the current rebound in environmental concerns is "not coming from nowhere," but wants to find out whether "this is a moment, or a movement."

Keith Brooks, programs director of Canadian environmental advocacy organization Environmental Defence, said he hopes the rebounding concern is a movement — and that interest continues to grow.

"I think support for climate action has never gone away, it's just that other things came in as more of an urgent priority," he said. "I'm hoping that people are grasping the severity of the climate crisis and the fact that it is definitely not going away."

WATCH | Former minister says wildfires are result of climate change: Wildfires, extreme weather are 'clearly climate change': former environment minister | Duration 8:48 Former minister of environment and climate change Catherine McKenna says the extreme weather across Canada and around the world is clearly due to climate change. She shares how Canadians can be protected right now, how to put climate change back on the political agenda and how advancing renewable technology may offer hope in moving away from fossil fuels.

Brooks said he would like to see a "complete about-face" from the federal government on climate and the environment. He said Carney "has not done good things" on climate change, rolling back on some of the previous government's environmental policies.

"The affordability crisis is a real crisis," Brooks said. "All of these things are legitimate concerns that people should be afraid about, but climate change is among those concerns.…

"Just because something's not someone's top concern doesn't mean it's not a concern and it doesn't mean that it doesn't need to be taken seriously by governments."

World.title: 80 people died trying to get to Ceuta. In Europe, politics could eclipse the tragedy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In Ceuta, the small Spanish territory at the tip of North Africa where more than 72,000 people crossed from Morocco last week by swimming around the border, asylum seekers wait to learn what comes next.

Dozens were seen resting on a small beach on the outskirts of town this week, as the enclave's few shelters were full, mostly with women and children, according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.

Aid groups that were largely absent when exhausted swimmers first stumbled ashore now distribute food and water to those who were not forced to return to Morocco. (Moroccan nationals cannot claim asylum in Spain under an agreement designating Morocco a safe third country.)

While humanitarian organizations respond to the aftermath on the ground, the debate across Europe has largely been about how to prevent another mass crossing.

European lawmakers debated the Ceuta crossings and migration policy in Brussels on Wednesday, after last week's events triggered one of the bloc's sharpest political disputes over migration in years.

Within hours of the crossings last week, member states of the European Union rushed to blame Spain, saying decisions by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez 's government had encouraged migrants to attempt the journey.

Italy temporarily suspended passport-free Schengen travel arrangements with Spain, even though they do not apply to Ceuta. And 22 of the European Union's 27 member states called for stronger external border controls.

WATCH | Hundreds of migrants are stuck in Ceuta: Ceuta faces humanitarian challenge after surge of migrants | Duration 2:06 Roughly 2,000 migrants are left in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after 70,000 surged into the autonomous city last week, leaving humanitarian organizations stretched to their limits.

European Commission President Ursula Von der Leyen called the crossings "unacceptable," and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz demanded Morocco "take back illegal migrants immediately."

Yesterday's meeting shifted the rhetoric of the past week somewhat, with interior ministers releasing a statement in solidarity with Spain and condemning attempts to divide the bloc.

But the sentiment remains. Over the weekend, new British Prime Minister Andy Burnham visited Dover, where asylum seekers land after crossing the Channel from France on boats. His visit came after Reform UK Leader Nigel Farage said that if elected, he would employ the Royal Navy to return migrants crossing the Channel back to France.

Migrants wait at a beach in Ceuta on Aug. 3 following deadly mass crossings of migrants on foot and by sea from Morocco into the Spanish territory. (Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters)

The reactions to Ceuta are a reflection not only of disagreements over migration policy but domestic political calculations, said Davide Colombi, a migration researcher at the Centre for European Policy Studies.

"Member states' governments are still acting according to their own national electorate," Colombi said, rather than in the interest of Europe. When they blamed Spain for the events in Ceuta, "they acted in their own defence rather than in co-operation."

Migrants seen as security threat

For José Javier Olivas, an associate professor of political science at Spain's UNED university, the significance of Ceuta lies in how it has been discussed.

He says politicians across Europe rapidly adopted language portraying the crossing as an "invasion," framing it as a security threat rather than a humanitarian emergency.

Migrants hold signs reading 'asylum' in Spanish while waiting in line to receive food and beverages from the Red Cross in Ceuta, Spain, on Aug. 3. (Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters)

"They have managed to impose the terms in which we discuss about the issue," Olivas said, arguing the far right's greatest victory was shifting the conversation away from the people still stranded in Ceuta.

Spain has increasingly found itself out of step with much of Europe on migration. Earlier this year, Prime Minister Sánchez expanded a program allowing 500,000 undocumented migrants, many of them from Latin America, already living in Spain to regularize their legal status.

Meanwhile, countries like Italy, Denmark and the Netherlands have emphasized migrant returns and tougher border enforcement. Colombi described Spain as "going in a very different direction" from many of its European partners.

Possibly misleading claims

Exactly what prompted tens of thousands of people to attempt the Ceuta crossing last week remains disputed.

Researchers point to a combination of misleading online claims, confusion over a recent Spanish Supreme Court ruling affecting return procedures for migrants arriving by sea and questions over Morocco's border enforcement.

Migrants wait outside Ceuta's temporary migrant centre (CETI), which is currently at full capacity, on Aug. 3. (Pedro Nunes/Reuters)

Colombi said there was evidence of widespread misinformation encouraging people to believe anyone reaching Ceuta would be allowed to remain in Spain, while adding that Morocco's precise role remains unclear.

In the days before the crossing, videos circulated widely on social media claiming migrants who reached Ceuta would not be deported. Other posts falsely suggested Spain's regularization program was about to close, creating a sense of urgency for people hoping to reach Europe.

Most of those videos have since been removed.

1,100 unaccompanied minors remain

European leaders are now focused on reinforcing borders instead of debating the fate of thousands of asylum seekers still awaiting legal assistance, shelter or asylum decisions, Olivas said.

"Very few people are talking about the fact that there are thousands of people still in the streets in Ceuta who don't have water, who don't have food, who don't know what's going to happen to them," he said.

Many of the remaining crossers are from other parts of Africa, having spent years travelling north in search of protection in Europe. In photographs taken by news agencies, some hold handmade reading "Asilo."

One Yemeni man who fled his country's civil war five years ago told El Pais he lost his brother in the sea near Ceuta. More than 80 people drowned or were crushed in last week's rush across the border, according to official figures.

Meanwhile, roughly 1,100 unaccompanied minors remain in Ceuta because they cannot be summarily deported, according to local authorities.

Many are staying in makeshift accommodation or sleeping rough as charities and neighbourhood groups struggle to care for children, pregnant women and others left stranded.

World.title: Backlash to OpenAI luxury retreat highlights influencers' uncertain relationship with AI
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

OpenAI hosted an all-expenses-paid gathering of content creators at an idyllic New York state resort last weekend — but the luxury getaway came at a cost for some attendees, who are now facing fierce fallout from followers for taking a promotional trip on the tech company's dime.

Some commenters took issue with influencers showing off the glamorous natural setting, reportedly in the Hudson Valley, despite concerns that OpenAI and other tech companies are having a significant impact on the environment and climate change . Others railed against the company’s work with the U.S. government, including the Department of War .

Influencer Grace McCarrick didn't think for a moment that taking part in what's known as a brand trip, to learn more about OpenAI's ChatGPT Work tools, would be controversial.

Addressing the backlash in a LinkedIn post, she said the response to her "awesome" time at the so-called summer camp had introduced her to "the shocking AI psychosis running rampant online," adding that she "genuinely had no idea that people were this anti-AI."

Experts say the uproar might not be solely about the pros and cons of artificial intelligence, but may also be a sign that content creators have come to a sort of crossroads when it comes to AI, tech giants and the unwritten bond of trust between them and their followers.

"Some of the criticism was obviously about people feeling it was in bad taste to be promoting a company like OpenAI," said Victoria Ibitoye, founder of the U.K.-based business website The Daily Influence.

"But I also think the reaction reflects the fact that the creator economy is still trying to figure out where it stands on AI more broadly."

WATCH | How artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how humans use the internet: Say goodbye to the internet as you know it | Duration 8:06 Artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping how humans use the internet. For The National, CBC’s Nora Young breaks down the future of search and what happens to information when bots do most of the reading online.

'Is that the cost of your soul?'

Ibitoye says it's clear OpenAI wanted to give content creators an opportunity to experience ChatGPT Work — billed as an AI agent that can automate workplace tasks by gathering information from applications and workflows — and then share its products with "audiences that already trust them."

But that clearly backfired for some who took part in the gathering.

Influencer Megan Lieu showcased her "2 days off the grid with OpenAI" on her LinkedIn and Instagram accounts, touting her experience as time well spent learning about ChatGPT's newest features, "all while taking in breathtaking views."

One commenter on Instagram called Lieu "a tool to be exploited by greedy white men," while another asked, "Is that the cost of your soul? One f---ing influencer trip."

McCarrick said on LinkedIn that "it was incredibly exciting to get to be in the room with the people shaping how this technology gets used," and appeared to call out the hypocrisy of some commenters.

"What gets my goat, honestly, is that every single of the commenters is on a smartphone. They're all on either Instagram or TikTok — two of the most addicting, extractive (if not straight up corrupt) platforms of our time."

Ibitoye says the uproar has "exposed the gap between what people say about AI and how they’re actually using it."

"People say they’re uncomfortable with AI, and I think many of those concerns are completely valid. But at the same time, AI is becoming increasingly embedded in how creators work and what audiences engage with. ... I don’t think the creator economy has fully reconciled those two things yet, and that’s why debates like this keep happening."

While brand trips in general can attract backlash because they often appear to be "over the top," Ibitoye says, much of the negative reaction in this case was centred on the influencers' collaboration with OpenAI specifically.

The San Francisco-based company was the "first mover" in the field of generative AI, explains Paris Marx, a St. John's-based tech writer and host of the podcast Tech Won't Save Us.

"And certainly Sam Altman, the CEO of the company, has also been very vocal, a very public figure in pushing and defending this technology."

AI's PR problem

Marx isn't surprised OpenAI lavished influencers with a weekend away in order "to say good things about their products," because the company is "very aware" that public opinion of it, and generative AI in general, isn't favourable.

"More and more people are questioning whether this industry is actually thinking about the kind of social benefit of their technologies or just about what they, at the end of the day, want to get out of it," he said.

LISTEN | How Canadians are responding to the rapid construction of data centres: Front Burner 28:16 Canada's data centre boom, and backlash

He points to recent Angus Reid polling that showed a majority of the Canadians surveyed (68 per cent) want the federal government to "heavily regulate" AI. That same poll found 67 per cent of respondents perceive AI data centres as bad for energy and environmental sustainability.

OpenAI is also facing accusations that ChatGPT played a role in suicides, and is facing potential legal action in British Columbia related to the mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge in February.

Influencer marketing and trust

OpenAI did not respond to a CBC News request for comment about the purpose of the luxury weekend, the number of influencers who attended, other details about the trip, and the backlash to it.

David Soberman, a marketing professor at the University of Toronto's Rotman School of Management, says some of the backlash may be rooted in the degree of knowledge people have about artificial intelligence.

But he says the outcry might also serve as a reminder that influencer marketing is not objective and that content creators may be more like traditional advertisers than their followers want to admit.

"People like to think that when they see an influencer, that this influencer is giving their honest opinion about these products," he said. "But they're not."

LISTEN | Can we keep AI from escaping human control? Ideas 54:00 How can we prevent AI from becoming a menace?

Ibitoye says influencers can take a paid trip from a company like OpenAI and still be critical of its products.

She says they take risk by appearing too cozy with a company.

"Trust is probably their most valuable currency," she said. "If they stop being honest with their audience, people notice."

World.title: As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

Hey, it's Bridget. I recently went to Vancouver Community College to visit their auto shop and learn about how they’re teaching apprentices about electric vehicles. I was curious about efforts to train the next generation of automotive technicians, so I decided to dig a little deeper.

This week:

As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?

The Big Picture: A landmark battery

This town tested a drone show as an animal-friendly alternative to fireworks

As more EVs hit the road, will we have the mechanics to keep them running?

Vancouver Community College instructor Mike Coard stands with some of the electric vehicles used to train apprentices in the school's Automotive Service Tech Department. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

EV sales are ramping up — not just cars but also trucks and buses. Canada wants EVs to make up 75 per cent of new vehicle sales by 2035 to help meet its goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 .

Electric school buses have gained traction in some parts of the country , but a new report suggests a challenge to keeping them running in the future — and it's one that could affect other EVs, too.

The report from the environmental think-tank Pollution Probe finds "key gaps" in training and certification of technicians to maintain and repair electric school buses.

Marc Saleh, Pollution Probe's director of transportation, said EVs require skills related to high-voltage safety, battery diagnostics, power electronics and charging infrastructure management that still aren't being taught in standard automotive service programs.

He and others in the auto service industry say this challenge applies not just to school buses but to all electric vehicles. There remain barriers to both training new automotive technicians and upgrading the skills of already certified Red Seal technicians.

Challenges for EV training

Saleh says technician training for EVs is primarily handled by manufacturers. But this will eventually need to change to properly support adoption, as there may soon be so many EVs that the dealerships can't service them all.

Emily Chung (no relation to the editor of this newsletter), president of the Automotive Industries Association of Canada, said what's involved in servicing an EV depends heavily on the make and model, because the location of components such as batteries varies more compared with components of internal combustion engine cars.

Pictured are two of the training aids that VCC instructor Mike Coard uses to teach students about batteries. On the left is a Tesla battery, and on the right is a hybrid battery pack from a Toyota Prius. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

"There's no standardization, even amongst the car manufacturers, and everybody started doing their own thing and have their own flavour," she said.

This is why she says proprietary technology is also an issue, because shops and classrooms don't always have access to all of the information needed to understand each vehicle.

Many manufacturers refuse to provide that access, or they charge extremely high fees that repair shops can't afford.

There is also no universal certification for EV training courses or any requirement for ongoing training after technicians receive a Red Seal certification — Canada's national standard for skilled trades such as automotive.

Some solutions

Despite these barriers, both independent auto shops and community colleges are trying to fill the gap.

Andrew Ackers owns a NAPA AutoPro shop in Hamilton.

He has been training technicians who are already familiar with traditional, internal combustion engine vehicles through an EV training program called Next Drive started by NAPA, an automotive co-operative that distributes replacement auto parts.

The program has five levels — there will be six starting in September — and goes from basic electrical theory all the way to diagnosing problems inside battery packs.

Ackers says it’s about a $20,000 investment per technician but is worth the price — and each level can be done in a week, meaning they don’t have to leave their jobs for long to complete the training.

"A strong technician that is comfortable with electrical work could be up to speed within a week's worth of training to be able to handle about 90 per cent of the high-voltage repairs that are necessary on vehicles," he said.

Ackers said he's dedicated about 15 per cent of his business to electric vehicles.

Vancouver Community College trains students on a variety of EVs and hybrids. In the shop is a Ford Fusion, Tesla Model 3, Nissan Leaf, Volkswagen ID.4, Rivian pickup truck and a Toyota Mirai. (Bridget Stringer-Holden/CBC)

Colleges are also stepping up to expand their clean energy programs and prepare technicians for the growing demand of EV repairs.

Vancouver Community College already has some training in place but is expanding the school’s offerings in September. To accommodate that, it is building a new Centre for Clean Energy that is scheduled to be completed in 2027. It will include space to train refrigeration technicians and electricians who will need to work on charging infrastructure.

Centennial College in Ontario is also expanding its offerings to help upskill existing Red Seal certified technicians and train new apprentices.

Pollution Probe's report recommends integrating electric vehicle content into trade curricula, and Michael Lomnicki, a professor in the School of Transportation and a Red Seal mechanic, said that's exactly what they’re working on at Centennial College.

"There's careers to be had, absolutely," he said. "I definitely think that it's important to invest in, so that all of our students can create value for themselves and lead this industry as technology evolves."

Chung of the Automotive Industries Association of Canada says this is a crucial component of the EV transition.

"Repairing and maintaining these cars is the most sustainable solution, right?" she said. "And so it goes hand in hand with the whole thought of being eco-friendly and moving towards clean energy."

– Bridget Stringer-Holden

Old issues of What on Earth? are here . The CBC News climate page is here .

Check out our podcast and radio show. In our latest episode : Flood-prone communities are doing everything to keep water out. But as climate-fuelled storms become more severe, some architects say we need to work with water, not fight it. We learn how amphibious engineering kept Bangladeshi kids in school and allowed a Louisiana community to stay afloat.

LISTEN | What if your home could float when a flood hits?: What On Earth 23:10 What if your home could float when a flood hits?

What On Earth drops new podcast episodes every Wednesday and Saturday. You can find them on your favourite podcast app or on demand at CBC Listen . The radio show airs Sundays at 11 a.m., 11:30 a.m. in Newfoundland and Labrador.

Check the CBC News Climate Dashboard for live updates on record-breaking weather and current conditions across the country. Set your location to find out how today's temperatures compare to historical trends.

(CBC)

Reader feedback

Last week, Emily Chung wrote about Canadian technology to cool subway stations , with the goal of recovering the heat in the future.

David Fujiwara wrote: "That’s great that energy efficient chilled water will be used in the East Broadway subway station, but nowhere do you tell us where that chilled water is coming from. If you are chilling the water with electric refrigeration is it so energy efficient? And if [the system] doesn’t yet have a district heat system to connect to, where is excess heat going in the interim?"

Yes, the system uses electric refrigeration. As mentioned in the article, because it is passive cooling without fans, it is expected to be 25 to 35 per cent more efficient and more compact than a traditional air conditioning system. During the pilot, the excess heat will be measured and vented above ground. But both the MTA and Cascara Energy are interested in making use of it in the future, to heat water (such as swimming pools) and buildings.

Write us at whatonearth@cbc.ca (and send photos there, too!)

The Big Picture: A landmark battery

(John Laytner/Civic Grid)

Stationary batteries are becoming a bigger part of our electricity system, helping support the use of clean but intermittent energy such as wind and solar . Batteries can store power when it's plentiful, feed extra power onto the grid when supplies are short and provide backup power during outages. But where should those batteries go?

Distributed energy storage firm Civic Grid argues they should be close to where people live and use the power. The photo above shows an example of its vision — a pilot project launched Wednesday in Cannington, Ont. The 60 kW battery is lit up beside the building on the right "transforming an invisible piece of electrical infrastructure into a public landmark," the company says. Its goal is to explore how energy storage can "move beyond industrial sites and become part of the communities it serves."

The battery is charged from the grid at night when power is plentiful. During the day, it can supply up to six hours of power to two buildings used by the Nourish and Develop Foundation, which provides local food and social services (on the right and at the back of the photo). It also supplies lighting to a privately owned public square on the property, including a sheltered seating area (back left).

— Emily Chung

Hot and bothered: Provocative ideas from around the web

The presence of cougars in a region can reduce the risk of car crashes, a new study finds. Here's how .

A U.S. company has effectively brought a geothermal well back from the dead to become one of the most productive pumped geothermal wells in the country.

Do small, individual green habits like recycling and taking transit distract people from taking bigger, more meaningful action? Or do they prime people to support or participate in larger climate initiatives? A new study may have solved this debate .

Big industrial offshore wind farms can impact wildlife such as birds that can fly into them. But researchers are finding they also provide habitat to creatures, from oyster larvae to porpoises. Atmos brings you up close to some of these wind farm dwellers .

This town tested a drone show as an animal-friendly alternative to fireworks

Images of fireworks, seen in a screenshot from a YouTube video, were among those created by 100 drones as an alternative to fireworks in the Town of Three Rivers, P.E.I., on Aug. 1. (H3xan01c/YouTube)

The Town of Three Rivers in P.E.I. replaced fireworks with a drone light show for its summer festival this year.

The town's Montague Arts and Culture Festival on Aug. 1 featured acclaimed P.E.I. singer-songwriter Lennie Gallant, along with what the town believes to be Prince Edward Island’s first-ever drone light show instead of a traditional fireworks display.

Jonathon Gardner, events and facilities co-ordinator for the Town of Three Rivers, said the idea began with an email from P.E.I. CARES — the Companion Animal Rescue Education Society — outlining some of the downsides of fireworks.

"There were quite a few reasons why fireworks aren't great for the environment and animals and people," Gardner told Mainstreet P.E.I. host Nicola MacLeod.

"Originally, we thought it was going to be far too expensive as well.... After looking into it, it was mildly affordable and [we] thought it would be a really neat change."

The show used 100 illuminated drones to create animated images and patterns in the night sky, synchronized to music.

WATCH | A YouTube video that captured the drone show:

Gardner said there is also growing awareness of how fireworks can affect people who are sensitive to noise, including those who have post-traumatic stress disorder.

"With our first responders or military, the amount of PTSD, absolutely, that could trigger [it]," he said.

Karla Shalley, founder and president of P.E.I. CARES, said the organization sent the same email to every municipality on P.E.I., hoping to encourage communities to rethink fireworks.

"We know what a thunderstorm causes with animals. Imagine that tenfold with fireworks," she said.

The P.E.I. Humane Society has also welcomed the move.

Ashley Travis, the organization's development and communications co-ordinator, said it regularly sees the fallout from fireworks displays.

"Nearly every year when there's a community fireworks display, we will receive a call from someone who either wasn't aware that there was going to be fireworks that evening or who perhaps brought their animal to a fireworks display," she said.

"There have been incidents where animals have fled, and ... we've seen animals get seriously injured when fleeing from loud noises like fireworks."

People often forget that what feels festive to humans can be frightening for animals, Travis said.

"Your animal does not know what's going on. They don't understand what a firework is. They just hear a very loud noise, an explosion. They can see very bright lights sometimes and it can be very, very scary for them," she said.

"We always say that the best-case scenario is to leave your pet at home during a fireworks display to make sure that they're going to be safe."

Both Travis and Shalley hope other communities will now consider alternatives to fireworks.

Ahead of the show, Gardner said the reaction from the community was encouraging.

"There’s been a lot of positive feedback. Lots of people are saying, 'I want to come and check it out, and I want to see it,'" he said.

— Thinh Nguyen

World.title: 'He just didn't deserve it': N.S. man sues province, health authority over son's death in custody
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An Annapolis Valley man is suing Nova Scotia's attorney general and the provincial health authority following his son's death this spring from an illness while in the province's custody.

Brandon Hendershot, 40, died of influenza B on April 16 at Dartmouth General Hospital, according to a statement of claim filed Thursday in Nova Scotia Supreme Court.

“My son is dead because we trusted the system and he just, he didn't deserve … he just didn't deserve it. Not him,” Brian Hendershot said in an interview with CBC News.

“They're supposed to protect you.”

Brandon Hendershot was arrested in Saskatchewan in early March and transported to Nova Scotia, where he was charged with two counts of sexual interference, two counts of sexual assault and one count of invitation to sexual touching.

His father alleges in the lawsuit that correctional staff failed to conduct a health assessment when his son arrived at the Central Nova Scotia Correctional Facility in Dartmouth in March and that they failed to provide adequate medical care while he was in custody.

Brandon Hendershot, left, and his father, Brian Hendershot. (Submitted by Brian Hendershot)

Brian Hendershot filed the lawsuit on behalf of himself and Brandon Hendershot’s teenage son.

Asked for comment, the province's Justice Department replied with a written statement.

“Our hearts always go out to the families and loved ones of people who die in custody," the statement said. "As this matter is before the courts, we cannot comment at this time.”

Nova Scotia Health declined a request for comment.

None of the allegations in the lawsuit have been tested in court and no statements of defence have yet been filed.

Calls for legislative change

Emma Halpern, the co-founder and legal director of non-profit law firm PATH Legal, is representing Brian Hendershot in the lawsuit. She’s calling on the province to be more transparent and proactive about deaths in custody.

In 2023, the Justice Department established a committee to review deaths in custody. Its mandate includes providing a report and recommendations any time someone dies in provincial custody.

The committee has since released two reports. One was three pages long and the other consisted of two pages.

Halpern says it’s not enough.

"It's very unclear how the people end up on that committee and what they're actually doing and how many meetings they have and what documents they get and what they're investigating,” Halpern said in an interview.

Emma Halpern is the co-founder and legal director of non-profit law firm PATH Legal. (CBC)

According to information on the Justice Department website, nine people have died in provincial custody since January 2023.

Four of those deaths — including Brandon Hendershot's — occurred this year. In accordance with the province’s Personal Health Information Act, no information about the nature of the other three deaths is available publicly.

Halpern said she’d like to see provincial legislation requiring in-depth inquests into every death in custody.

“I'm deeply troubled by what I see as a pattern of deaths occurring within our jails,” she said.

Justice Minister Scott Armstrong says he’s satisfied the current system gives the province the information it needs to make necessary changes to how correctional facilities operate.

"If I saw a trend, for example, and certain things causing these deaths in custody, then we'd probably take some steps to do a further investigation," he told reporters Thursday.

Justice Minister Scott Armstrong takes questions from reporters on Thursday, Aug. 6, 2026. (CBC)

He said there are a number of reasons why someone could die in custody.

"It could just be natural causes," he said.

Hendershot’s death is listed on the Justice Department’s incident database as a death of natural causes. Halpern said, however, that it was entirely preventable.

"Clearly, Brandon needed the course of antibiotics. Why didn't he get that?"

Inquest model

Meaghan Daniel, whose law firm's focuses include prison law, has concerns about the province's death review committee process.

“What the Nova Scotia model seems to be saying is that just the public disclosure of the lesson learned is sufficient,” she said in an interview.

“But we haven't learned the problem that led to it. And so that to me is problematic.”

Daniel said the underlying theory of an inquest is based on the idea that public understanding of a death is itself a form of accountability. She said inquests like those carried out in Ontario after a death in custody provide families and the public with valuable information.

“What these families want is meaning to be made from the loss. The very particular loss of someone they love,” she said.

Brian Hendershot said that after his son's death, he picked up his belongings from the Dartmouth jail and had a brief chat with the facility’s clergyman.

He said he’s heard little from the province on the matter and wants answers about why his son died.

Hendershot is suing for damages for pain and suffering and loss of amenities, along with aggravated and punitive damages. No specific dollar amount is included in the lawsuit.

World.title: 8 dead in Thailand as teen shoots grandparents, then students
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Thai teenager killed at least five people and himself at a ‌school outside Bangkok on Friday after fatally shooting his grandparents, police said, in the Southeast Asian nation's worst mass killing since 2022.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff and police said the 14-year-old shooter, a student, fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that belonged to his grandfather. Police said 23 people were injured.

Students streamed out of the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, on the capital's northwestern outskirts, as the wounded were loaded on to ambulances and teachers hugged each other and cried. In photos circulated by emergency workers, one person is seen lying down on a stretcher outside an ambulance, while another is attended to ​by a medic.

One 18-year-old student told Reuters he initially thought there were firecrackers going off or someone banging an object.

"I didn't think it was a gun at first," he said. "There were many ​shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again."

Lt.-Gen. Trairong Phophan, a spokesman for the National Police, told Reuters ⁠the suspected shooter was among the seven ⁠people killed at the school. Fifteen people were injured, he added.

Thai PM expresses condolences

Education Minister Prasert ‌Jantararuangtong told Reuters that both teachers and students were among the casualties. Police identified the perpetrator as a student.

It is the second school shooting in Thailand this year after a teacher died and a student was injured in the south of the country in February.

Police stand outside the home of the student suspected of shooting several people. (Sakchai Lalit/The Associated Press)

Emergency worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, 47, described arriving as the shooting was ongoing and his team treated students with injuries in the back, chest and arms. They found a male teacher lying dead on ⁠an upper floor of the school, and in another room they found a female teacher with wounds in her chest and arm.

He said he was called to treat the teenage shooter after hearing a final shot.

"We rushed up and found that the perpetrator had shot himself in the right side of the head and collapsed. When we got up there, we checked ‌his pulse, he still had one, so we started CPR."

The suspect was then taken to the hospital, he said.

In the 2025 academic year, the school had an enrolment of around 3,100 students and 147 teachers, according to district authorities.

"This is terrible for something like this to happen," Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters. "I'm sad for those who died and sad for something like this to happen in our country."

Gun ownership and gun violence are not uncommon in ​Thailand, which has seen a series of deadly shootings in the past six years, with children among the victims.

Thailand's worst mass killing by a single perpetrator in its recent history took place in 2022, when a former policeman ran amok ⁠in a three-hour gun-and-knife attack in the northeast that killed 36 people including 22 children stabbed as they slept at a daycare centre.

After a 2023 shooting in which a 14-year-old used a modified handgun to kill two people and wound ​five others at a luxury Bangkok shopping centre, Thailand ordered a raft of gun control measures, including a short-term ban on new licences, import restrictions and banning of people under 20 years from shooting ranges.

Longer-term measures also included a medical certificate assessing the mental health and psychological condition of gun owners as well as a specified validity period for some gun licenses.

Thailand had an estimated 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, equating to around 15 guns per 100 residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small ⁠Arms Survey.
