World.title: Former governor of Guerrero arrested on Ayotzinapa-related charges
World.content:
Federal authorities on Thursday announced the arrest of former Guerrero Governor Ángel Heladio Aguirre Rivero in connection with the 2014 abduction and presumed murder of 43 teachers college students.

Aguirre, governor of Guerrero from 2011 until his resignation in October 2014, was detained in México state on charges of concealment and/or destruction of evidence related to the whereabouts of the students, according to the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR).

“Ángel Aguirre”:

Porque fue detenido por su presunta participación en el ocultamiento de evidencias de Ayotzinapa pic.twitter.com/00qyDYyn1J — ¿Por qué es Tendencia? (@porktendencia) August 6, 2026

The FGR said on social media on Thursday morning that “as part of a new investigative model,” it carried out a reexamination of the September 2014 disappearance of 43 students from the Ayotzinapa Rural Teachers College in Guerrero. The students — all young men — disappeared in Iguala, Guerrero, on September 26, 2014, after the bus on which they were traveling to Mexico City was stopped by municipal and state police.

Police allegedly handed the students over to members of Guerreros Unidos, a crime gang.

The FGR said that “new acts of investigation” allowed it to “confirm the possible participation” of Aguirre, a Democratic Revolution Party governor, “in the concealment of evidence” related to the whereabouts of the students.

Consequently, a warrant for the arrest of the ex-governor was “requested, obtained and executed,” the FGR said on Thursday morning.

The FGR subsequently released a statement from Attorney General Ernestina Godoy, who said that the FGR has evidence that Aguirre ordered the concealment of video footage that showed the bus on which the students were traveling at the time it was stopped by police.

“On the night of September 26, 2014, the ‘Estrella de Oro’ bus number 1531, on which the group of teacher-training students was traveling, was captured on video by security cameras 12 and 15, located outside the State Palace of Justice in Iguala, at the time it was stopped by municipal and state police officers,” Godoy said.

“The first official statements claimed that the material in question did not exist due to alleged technical failures in the [security camera] system. However, subsequent investigations confirmed that this claim was false,” she said.

Godoy said that in January, a cooperating witness provided testimony that “confirmed the existence of the video recordings.” That witness, the attorney general said, identified the person who “removed” the recordings in order to “deliver them directly” to Aguirre.

Godoy said that the witness also provided information about threats they had received, which “explained their previous silence.”

The attorney general said that in May, “a second protected witness strengthened said testimony” by declaring that Aguirre “ordered, in a meeting with top officials from his government,” the concealment of “any evidence related to the events that occurred in the vicinity of the Iguala Palace of Justice.”

“The Attorney General’s Office has evidence that confirms that said instruction of concealment was issued directly by the then governor, with the participation of high-level state public servants,” Godoy said.

Near the start of her statement, the attorney general said that a reexamination of the Ayotzinapa case “confirmed with full evidence and adherence to due process the possible participation of Ángel ‘N,’ ex-governor of the state of Guerrero, in the destruction of evidence [needed] to determine the whereabouts of the students.”

Godoy said that Aguirre was arrested on Thursday in México state, but didn’t specify exactly where he was taken into custody. However, according to the National Arrests Register, the ex-governor was detained on Thursday morning in Tepotzotlán, a México state municipality north of Mexico City. He was subsequently transferred to the Altiplano federal prison in Almoloya de Juárez, México state.

The arrest of Aguirre is one of the most prominent detentions in connection with the Ayotzinapa case, which sparked outrage in Mexico and around the world, and triggered large protests in Mexico City and across the country.

In a 2023 report, the previous federal government led by former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador outlined three “possible reasons” for the abduction of the students, one of which was “the possible presence of drugs, weapons or money” on buses Ayotzinapa students had commandeered to travel to a protest in Mexico City.

The disappearance of the 43 young men — a “crime of the state,” according to a top official in the previous federal government — was a major blight on the 2012-18 presidency of Enrique Peña Nieto, but he survived widespread calls for his removal from office. The remains of just three students have been found.

Scores of people have been arrested in connection with the case, but no has been convicted of the crime and some suspects have been released from prison. Among those who have been detained are soldiers and high-ranking members of the Mexican Army, police officers, Guerreros Unidos members and Jesús Murillo Karam, federal attorney general at the time of the students’ disappearance.

Murillo was detained in 2022 on charges of forced disappearance, torture and obstruction of justice in connection with the Aytozinapa case. He was released from prison in 2024 after a judge ruled he could await trial under house arrest. The 78-year-old former attorney general suffered a stroke in April.

With reports from La Jornada and AP

World.title: Vatican envoy prays for Mexico’s missing at CDMX Basilica Mass
World.content:
Vatican Secretary of State Cardinal Pietro Parolin, who’s in Mexico as part of a multi-day official visit that began on Tuesday, presided a Mass at the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe in Mexico City, where he called for prayers for missing persons and “searching mothers.”

After reading a few passages from the Bible regarding the miracles of the Virgin Mary and concern for one’s neighbor, Pietro spoke of the arduous search undertaken by mothers with a missing loved one.

En Palacio Nacional, recibí al secretario de Estado del Vaticano, Pietro Parolin; abordamos temas como la primera encíclica del papa León XIV, Magnifica Humanitas, donde plantea que el desarrollo de la inteligencia artificial debe estar guiado por criterios éticos, dignidad… pic.twitter.com/HU7yc9S9Zp — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) August 5, 2026

“Their example resonates with particular force here in Mexico, where so many mothers continue to search for their missing children with steadfastness and faith,” he said, calling upon the faithful to support them with solidarity and prayer.

During his homily, Parolin noted that too many communities are “scarred by violence and aggression” and that a significant number of families have experienced the pain of loss. He urged that prayer be translated into concrete actions of solidarity with victims, migrants, and marginalized groups.

The Mass followed a one-hour meeting between Pietro and President Claudia Sheinbaum, during which both officials discussed the formal invitation for Pope Leo XIV to visit Mexico.

Sheinbaum reiterated her invitation for the pope to visit the country at her Wednesday morning press conference, saying, “We’re going to insist on the visit of the pope to Mexico.”

The meeting also addressed the challenges posed by artificial intelligence in light of Pope Leo XIV’s latest encyclical Dilexi Te.

“The Pope’s calls for peace, fraternity, and closeness to the most vulnerable represent a humanitarian vision—one that is indispensable at a time when the world needs to strengthen dialogue, solidarity, and cooperation among nations,” Sheinbaum wrote on her official X account along with a picture of the meeting.

The message of the pope’s emissary carries significant weight in Mexico, the country with the second-highest Catholic population in the world after Brazil. Nearly 80% of Mexico’s population (101.3 million people) identify as Roman Catholic.

Pietro’s statement comes as Mexico continues to confront a disappearance crisis, with over 132,000 people officially listed as missing or unaccounted for, and mothers and relatives often leading the search themselves.

With reports from El Universal and Vatican News

World.title: Reward for CJNG’s new leader jumps to $25 million after ‘El Mencho’s’ death
World.content:
The U.S. government on Wednesday raised from US $5 million to $25 million the maximum reward it is offering for information leading to the arrest of Juan Carlos Valencia González, the alleged new leader of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG).

The U.S. State Department announced the higher bounty as part of reward offers totaling up to $102 million “for information leading to the arrests and/or convictions, in any country, of eight leaders and associates” of the CJNG, one of eight Mexican criminal organizations that have been designated as foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs) by the U.S. government. All of the eight people — seven men and one woman — face criminal charges in the United States.

“The reward offers include up to $25 million (an increase from up to $5 million) for Juan Carlos Valencia González, aka ‘Pelón,’ the new leader of CJNG following the recent death of his stepfather, CJNG founder Nemesio Rubén Oseguera Cervantes, aka ‘El Mencho,'” the State Department said in a statement titled “Degrading CJNG: Announcing over $100 Million in Reward Offers and Visa Restrictions.”

Oseguera, the founder of the CJNG and longtime leader of the powerful cartel, was fatally wounded by soldiers during a military operation in Tapalpa, Jalisco, on Feb. 22.

His 41-year-old stepson — a California native who is also known as “El R3,” among other aliases — was subsequently identified in media reports as a leading contender to become the new leader of the CJGN.

According to an online Department of State wanted poster, Valencia González was charged in October 2020 in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia with “conspiracy to distribute a controlled substance for purpose of unlawful importation into the United States and use of a firearm during a narcotics transaction.”

US raises reward for a suspect already in custody

The U.S. State Department announced a reward of up to $15 million — an increase from up to $5 million — for the conviction of Audias Flores Silva, aka “El Jardinero” (The Gardener), who was detained by the Mexican Navy in Nayarit in April.

Prior to his capture, the 45-year-old Michoacán native was a “regional commander” of the CJNG, according to the State Department.

“In addition to his narco-trafficking activities, Flores Silva is the alleged leader of CJNG’s timeshare fraud operations in Nayarit, including a major operation centered around the Kovay Gardens resort targeting vulnerable Americans,” the State Department said in an online poster.

“… The U.S. Department of State is offering a reward increase of up to $15 million for information leading to the conviction of Flores Silva,” the State Department said.

Rewards of $2 million to $15 million for 6 other suspects

The State Department said it is also offering a reward of up to $15 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction of Gonzalo Mendoza Gaytán, aka “El Sapo” (The Toad), who is said to be a godson of Oseguera.

Mendoza is a “senior leader” of the CJNG and “controls most of the cartel’s operations in Jalisco,” according to the State Department. The 37-year-old Michoacán native was also mentioned in media reports as a possible successor to “El Mencho.”

The State Department is also offering a reward of up to $15 million for information leading to the capture and/or conviction of Julio Alberto Castillo Rodríguez, a son-in-law of the now-deceased Oseguera.

Castillo, known as “Chorro” and “Ojo de Vidrio” (Glass Eye), is a “senior member” of the CJNG and runs the cartel’s “daily operations in Colima, including by exercising control over parts of the port of Manzanillo, one of Mexico’s busiest ports,” according to the State Department. The 49-year-old is also a native of Michoacán, the state where “El Mencho” was born.

The State Department is offering rewards of up to $10 million each for Ricardo Ruiz Velasco, aka “Tripa” and “Doble R”; Julio César Montero Pinzón, aka “El Tarjetas”; and Carlos Andrés Rivera Varela, aka “La Firma.”

Ruiz, who was also mentioned in media reports as a possible successor to Oseguera, is a senior CJNG “lieutenant” and “leader of ‘Grupo Élite,’ a CJNG paramilitary group known for its extreme violence,” according to the State Department.

Montero is an “alleged high-ranking leader” of the CJNG who “allegedly directed an international complex fraud scheme targeting Americans who own timeshare properties in Mexico.”

Rivera, a native of Colombia, is “an alleged high-ranking leader” of the CJNG who also “allegedly directed an international complex fraud scheme targeting Americans who own timeshare properties in Mexico,” according to the State Department.

The State Department is offering a reward of up to $2 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction of Griselda Margarita Arredondo Pinzón, an “alleged high-ranking financial operator” for the CJNG. She is Montero’s half-sister, according to U.S authorities.

State Department announces US visa restrictions on relatives and associates of people linked to CJNG

In the same statement, the State Department announced that it was “imposing visa restrictions on 65 individuals who are family members or close personal or business associates of persons linked to CJNG” and who have been sanctioned under Executive Order 14059: Imposing Sanctions on Foreign Persons Involved in the Global Illicit Drug Trade.

It said that 26 of those individuals “had existing visas, which have now been revoked.”

“Since announcing this visa restriction policy in June 2025, a total of 93 visas have been revoked from family members and associates of sanctioned drug traffickers connected to FTO-designated cartels,” the State Department said.

“Under President Trump and Secretary Rubio’s leadership, violent cartel operatives and their criminal facilitators are no longer able to enter our country and terrorize the American people.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio took to social media on Wednesday to tout the new rewards and visa restrictions.

“The United States is hunting down, dismantling, and destroying Cártel de Jalisco Nueva Generación,” he wrote on X.

U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ron Johnson shared Rubio’s X post, writing above it:

“The pressure on the cartels and narcoterrorist organizations continues. … Under the leadership of @POTUS @realDonaldTrump, working alongside Mexican authorities, we are dismantling cartel leadership and holding accountable those who traffic deadly narcotics, such as fentanyl, and spread violence.”

The pressure on the cartels and narcoterrorist organizations continues. The United States announced criminal charges targeting senior CJNG leaders and more than $100 million in rewards for information leading to their capture. Under the leadership of @POTUS @realDonaldTrump,… https://t.co/2rfbMleFpT — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) August 5, 2026

A blow to the CJNG in Spain

Separately, the National Police of Spain (CNP) announced on Wednesday that its agents, in a joint operation with the French Anti-Narcotics Office OFAST, had “broken up a branch of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG) allegedly dedicated to the international trafficking of methamphetamine, and dismantled all its logistics infrastructure in Spain, including a clandestine laboratory.”

Thirteen people who allegedly belong to the criminal group were detained in operations in the cities of Lleida, Barcelona and Tarragona. Seven Mexicans, four Spaniards and two Colombians were arrested in the three cities, all of which are located in the Catalonia region of northeastern Spain.

The CNP said that the CJNG cell allegedly brought into Spain from Mexico “2.5 tonnes of methamphetamine camouflaged in approximately 12 tonnes of liquid vanilla flavoring.”

The confiscation of the meth was “one of the largest seizures” ever in Spain and Europe, the CNP said.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: How Guanajuato set the stage for Mexico’s independence from Spain
World.content:
The state of Guanajuato brings local and foreign tourists alike interested in exploring famous colonial towns and unique nature. But behind the manicured streets of San Miguel de Allende and Guanajuato City lie some of the most important stories in Mexican history.

On Sept. 28, 1810, Miguel Hidalgo y Castillo marched into Guanajuato with a ragtag army of tens of thousands at his back, kicking off the Mexican War of Independence. But why did it start here?

Just 12 days earlier in the town of Dolores, located approximately 60 kilometers from the capital city, Hidalgo issued his famous cry. The priest was fed up with Spanish colonial rule, which had conquered Mexico nearly 300 years prior. The cry was an urge to the people of Hidalgo’s congregation. He was pleading with them to revolt against the Spanish, and called his parish to arms.

The speech worked, and days later Hidalgo was the commander of an unofficial, untrained and unruly army, tens of thousands of soldiers strong. They were peasants, laborers and the poor. They had little equipment and even less training, but they had numbers.

The peasant army marched from Dolores to San Miguel de Allende and down to Celaya, where they looted and sacked Spanish homes, bringing more Indigenous and Creole people into their ranks.

Hidalgo’s forces reached Guanajuato with little resistance. Juan Antonio Riaño, the Spanish intendant of Guanajuato, chose to fight instead of surrendering the city. Riaño barricaded himself in the Alhóndiga de Granaditas, a massive, fortified stone structure made for storing grain.

Riaño’s force of around 400 men was greatly outnumbered. Spanish families moved into the granary, their wealth and belongings in tow, hoping to find shelter from the revolutionary horde. However, Riaño’s decision to only shelter Spanish families angered the local population in Guanajuato, who rallied behind Hidalgo.

With a massive force now ranging from 20,000 to 50,000 men, Hidalgo began the siege. He ordered his men to charge the gates of the fortress, where they took heavy losses but began to pound the front gate.

Riaño, now sensing defeat, tried to leave with a group of soldiers, but was shot and killed instantly. Riaño was previously a close friend of Hidalgo, who even wrote to Riaño before the siege to offer protection of him and his family, but the Spaniard had rejected — a decision which cost him his life.

The Spanish, however, still had one trick up their sleeve. They fitted a rifle with a white flag and waved it from the roof of the granary, signaling surrender. But as the rebellious forces began to drop their guard and approach the gates, the order was rescinded and the Spanish gunned down the unsuspecting soldiers.

It was too little too late, however, as the fortress was breached by insurgent soldier Juan José de los Reyes Martínez Amaro, the unlikeliest of heroes. A local miner — whose appearance, according to legend, resembled a turkey or guajolote, giving rise to the nickname “El Pípila” — strapped a large stone to his back and approached the gate with tar and a torch. The stone shielded him from gunfire, and he was able to burn through the door.

El Pípila’s statue now stands high above the city at Guanajuato’s famous viewpoint. He is honored for his bravery and as a hero of the city.

With the gate open, Hidalgo’s forces flew inside and mercilessly slaughtered the Spanish, including the huddled families who entered the granary seeking shelter. Their wealth was pillaged and the violence spread into the streets, where the resistance army spent days destroying Spanish and Creole homes and stealing their possessions. Over 3,000 insurgents were killed during the siege and the ensuing violence, along with hundreds of Spanish in the granary.

The attack on Guanajuato was brutal, but the rebels had won the first battle of the War of Independence. Hidalgo continued to lead his forces through the Bajío, and the battle set the stage for Mexican victory, with the Spanish abandoning the country in 1821.

The bullet holes from the siege are still riddled throughout the walls of the granary. They serve as both a reminder of the fight that led to a free Mexico and a monument to the lives lost from war.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: The peso’s wildest swings since 2000
World.content:
Anyone who has been living in or visiting Mexico for an extended period of time knows that at certain times this century, one US dollar bought significantly fewer Mexican pesos than it does today.

I’m talking about 25 years ago, 20 years ago, 15 years ago.

I’m not talking about 10 years ago, when the greenback rose above 20 to the peso, or six years ago, when the USD:MXN exchange rate exceeded 25 at the onset of the COVID pandemic.

At the close of trading on Aug. 5 (i.e. yesterday), one US dollar was worth 17.24 Mexican pesos, according to the Bank of Mexico. That puts the current USD:MXN exchange rate more or less on par with the prevailing rates in December 2015 and June 2023.

This “Mexico in Numbers” article will show you how the USD:MXN exchange rate has changed this century. The aim is not to examine in depth why the rate has changed over the past 25 years, although I do mention a few factors that have caused the peso to appreciate or depreciate at different times this century.

Before we look closely at the USD:MXN exchange rate fluctuations since Jan. 1, 2001, here are two key numbers relevant to our topic.

* N.B. — All of the USD:MXN exchange rate data in this article comes from the Bank of Mexico (Banxico). Exchange rate data from 1954 to 2026 can be downloaded from the central bank’s website.

25.12

This is the highest USD:MXN exchange rate this century, and indeed of all time. This was the prevailing rate on March 24, 2020 — 13 days after the World Health Organization declared the COVID-19 outbreak a pandemic.

8.94

This is the lowest USD:MXN exchange rate this century. This was the prevailing rate on May 21, 2001 — 113 days before two planes crashed into the Twin Towers in New York City.

Changes in the USD:MXN exchange rate this century

For each of the five-year intervals that appear below, I note the prevailing USD:MXN exchange rates on the first trading day of each year and on June 30 (or on the closest trading day to that date). I also highlight the highest and lowest exchange rates in each period.

2001-2005: The peso weakens almost 9%

The Mexican peso traded at 9.71 to the US dollar on Jan. 2, 2001, the second calendar day of this century. On June 29, 2001, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 9.07. Just over a month earlier, as noted above, the peso traded at 8.94 to the greenback, its strongest position this century.

On Jan. 2, 2002, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 9.10, while on July 1 of that year it was 9.92. On September 4, 2002, the USD:MXN exchange rate went above 10 for the first time this century. The peso previously traded at more than 10 to the dollar in 1998 and early 1999.

On Jan. 2, 2003, the peso traded 10.36 to the dollar, while on June 30 of that year the USD:MXN rate was 10.43.

On Jan. 2, 2004, the USD:MXN rate was 11.08, while on June 30 of that year it was 11.52. The USD:MXN exchange rate reached its highest point of the 2001-2005 period on May 10, 2004, when one greenback bought 11.63 pesos.

On Jan. 3, 2005, one US dollar was worth 11.20 pesos, while the USD:MXN rate was 10.77 on June 30 of that year and 10.63 on Dec. 30.

Thus, the peso depreciated 92 centavos, or around 8.7%, against the US dollar between Jan. 1, 2001 and Dec. 30, 2005. The peso’s weakest point in the period (11.63 to the dollar) represented a 23.1% depreciation compared to its strongest point (8.94).

2006-2010: The pace of peso depreciation quickens

The USD:MXN exchange rate on Jan. 2, 2006, was 10.62, while on June 30 it was 11.27.

On the first trading day of 2007 — Jan. 2 — one US dollar bought 10.78 pesos, while a greenback purchased 10.79 pesos on June 29 of that year.

On Jan. 2, 2008, the peso traded at 10.89 to the dollar, while on June 30 of that year the Mexican currency was stronger at 10.30 to the greenback. On Aug. 5, 2008, the peso reached its strongest position of the 2006-10 period, trading at 9.91 to the dollar.

On Jan. 2, 2009, the peso traded at a much weaker 13.76 to the dollar and exactly two months later, on March 2 , the currency fell to its weakest point of the 2006-10 period — 15.36 to the dollar at a time when the global financial crisis had taken a heavy toll on the Mexican currency. By June 30, 2009, the peso had significantly recovered to trade at 13.17 to the dollar.

On the first trading day of 2010 — Jan. 4 — the peso was even stronger at 12.92 to the dollar. The USD:MXN exchange rate was 12.84 on June 30, 2010, and 12.34 on Dec. 31 of that year.

The peso depreciated 13.9% between Jan. 2, 2006 and December 31, 2010. The peso’s weakest point in the period (15.36 to the dollar) represented a 55% depreciation compared to its strongest point (9.91). That wild swing occurred in the space of just seven months.

2011-2015: The pace of peso depreciation quickens again, doubling to almost 30%

On Jan. 3, 2011, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 12.25, while on June 30 of that year it was 11.72. The peso’s strongest point in this five-year period was a rate of 11.50 to the greenback on May 2, 2011.

On the first trading day of 2012 — Jan. 2 — the peso traded at 13.93 to the greenback, whereas on June 29 the USD:MXN rate was 13.40

On Jan. 2, 2013, the peso was stronger at 12.74 to the greenback, while on July 1 of that year it traded at 12.91 to the dollar.

On Jan. 2, 2014, one greenback bought 13.10 pesos, while on June 30 the peso was slightly stronger at 12.97 to the dollar.

On the first trading day of 2015 — Jan. 2 — the USD:MXN rate was 14.82, while the dollar was significantly stronger on June 30 of that year, buying 15.68 pesos. The greenback continued strengthening in the second half of 2015, reaching its strongest point of the 2011-15 period on Dec. 14, when it bought 17.37 pesos.

A week before the peso tumbled to that point, Reuters reported that the Mexican currency had fallen to “a more than two-month low” as crude oil prices hovered near 7-year lows. Then-Bank of Mexico Governor Agustín Carstens said at the time that global volatility could continue to hit the peso in December 2015. And Carstens was right — the peso depreciated further from the 16.90 rate on Dec. 7, 2015, the date on which his remarks to Reuters were published.

In the five years between January 2011 and December 31, 2015 — when the USD:MXN rate was 17.24 — the peso depreciated 28.9%. The peso’s weakest point in the period (17.37 to the dollar) represented a 33.8% depreciation compared to its strongest point (11.50).

2016-2020: Pandemic drags peso down to its weakest level ever

On Jan. 4, 2016, the USD: MXN exchange rate was 17.35, while on June 30, one greenback bought 18.46 pesos.

On April 29, 2016, the peso traded at its strongest level in the 2016-2020 period — 17.17 to the greenback. However, later in 2016 — on Nov. 10 to be exact — the peso traded above 20 to the dollar for the first time ever. The peso’s depreciation to above 20 to the dollar came two days after Donald Trump won the 2016 presidential election.

On Nov. 10, 2016, Reuters reported that the Mexican peso had sunk again, “taking its biggest two-day tumble in more than 20 years as investors worried about how U.S. president-elect Donald Trump’s policies could hit exports from Latin America’s second largest economy.”

Earlier in 2016, as the peso approached 20 to the dollar, memes appeared showing the Mexican 20-peso banknote with the words “new one-dollar bill” superimposed on it.

On the first trading day of 2017 — Jan. 2 — the peso was still above 20 to the dollar, with the USD:MXN rate at 20.73. On June 30 of that year, the peso was significantly stronger at 18.06 to the greenback.

On Jan. 2, 2018, the USD:MXN exchange rate was 19.48, while on June 30 of that year it was 19.69.

On Jan. 2, 2019, one greenback bought 19.58 pesos while on July 1 of that year a dollar purchased 19.07 pesos.

On the first trading day of 2020 — Jan. 2 — the peso traded at 18.88 to the dollar, while on June 30 it was significantly weaker at 23.08 to the greenback.

As noted at the start of this article, the peso depreciated to its weakest level ever — 25.12 to the dollar — on March 24, 2020, at the onset of the COVID pandemic.

On March 23, 2020, Mexico News Daily reported that the peso had fallen to “a new record low” against the US dollar “as the coronavirus pandemic continues to take a heavy toll on economies around the world.”

At the time, MND reported: “The financial group Monex said that the peso is facing ‘considerable stress’ due to the economic impact of COVID-19 around the world. As the pandemic worsens, investors have rushed to free themselves of high-risk currencies, such as the peso, in favor of the US dollar, which is regarded as the ultimate safe-haven currency.”

By the end of 2020, the peso had substantially recovered, trading at 19.90 to the dollar on Dec. 31.

Between January 2016 and December 2020, the peso depreciated 12.8%. The peso’s weakest point in the period (25.12 to the dollar) represented a 31.6% depreciation compared to its strongest point (17.17).

2021-2025: The value of the peso against the dollar goes up, not down!

On Jan. 4, 2021 — the first trading day of this decade — the USD:MXN exchange rate was 19.84, while on June 30 of that year one dollar bought 19.90 pesos. Later in the year, on Nov. 26, the peso depreciated to its weakest level in the 2021-25 period — 21.82 to the greenback.

By the end of 2021, the peso had recovered somewhat to trade at 20.46 on Dec. 31. On that date, Reuters reported that the peso had gained “to above one-month highs … amid fewer concerns about the economic impact of a rise in coronavirus infections.”

Three days later, on Jan. 3, 2022, the peso traded at 20.58 to the dollar, while the USD:MXN exchange rate on June 30 of that year was 20.13.

On the first trading day of 2023 — Jan 2. — the peso traded at 19.48 to the greenback, an appreciation of over 3% for the Mexican currency compared to six months earlier. On June 30, 2023, the peso was significantly stronger again at 17.13 to the dollar.

At various times later in the year, the peso traded at below 17 to the dollar. MND reported on July 12, 2023, that the peso had “strengthened to 16.82 to the US dollar … on the back of data that showed that annual inflation in the United States slowed to 3% in June [of that year], its lowest level in over two years.”

On the first trading day of 2024, the peso was back above 17 to the dollar, but only just. On Jan. 2 of that year, the peso traded at 17.02 to the dollar, while on July 1, 2024, the USD:MXN rate was 18.38.

On April 8, 2024 — the day that a total solar eclipse mesmerized millions across Mexico — the peso appreciated to its strongest point of the 2021-2025 period, trading at 16.33 to the greenback. On that day, MND reported that the peso had “continued its hot streak…, appreciating to its strongest level against the dollar in almost nine years.”

At the time, Banco Base’s director of economic analysis, Gabriela Siller, attributed the appreciation of the peso to three factors: the inflow to Mexico of foreign currencies from exports, remittances and foreign direct investment; the “expectation” that the wide gap between interest rates in Mexico and the United States (11% in the former vs. 5.25%-5.50% in the latter at the time) would “attract capital to Mexico”; and the “expectation” that nearshoring would “attract waves of dollars” to Mexico.”

By the time the first trading day of 2025 rolled around, the peso was significantly weaker, trading at 20.69 to the greenback on Jan. 2 of that year. On June 30, 2025, the peso was stronger at 18.83 to the dollar, while the currency finished the year at 18.00 to the greenback on Dec. 31.

Between January 2021 and the end of 2025, the peso appreciated 10.2% against the dollar. Of the five-year periods considered in this article — five in total — the 2021-2025 interval was the only one in which the peso appreciated against the dollar. In addition, it was the only interval in which the peso’s strongest position came after its weakest position. The peso’s strongest point in the period (16.33 to the dollar in April 2024) represented a 33.6% appreciation compared to its weakest point (21.82 in November 2021).

2026: The peso continues to strengthen

Compared to the Bank of Mexico’s closing rate on Dec. 31, 2025 of 18.00 Mexican pesos to the dollar, the peso has appreciated 4.4% this year, based on the 17.24 closing rate on Aug. 5.

The El Economista newspaper reported on Wednesday, Aug. 5, that the appreciation of the peso, after closing at 17.26 on Aug. 4, was “supported by a greater appetite for risk” as currency traders remained “attentive to news about a possible [peace] agreement in the Middle East,” where the United States and Iran have been at war since late February.

Key numerical takeaways from the changes in the USD:MXN exchange rate this century

Between Dec. 29, 2000 and Aug. 5, 2026 — this century, in other words — the Mexican peso depreciated 44.3%.

Put differently, the US dollar appreciated 79.6% between the end of 2000 and Aug. 5, 2026.

The difference between the highest USD:MXN rate this century (25.12) and the lowest (8.94) is 16.18 pesos.

Between May 21, 2001, the day the USD:MXN rate was 8.94, and March 24, 2020, the day that the USD:MXN rate was 25.12, the peso depreciated 64.4%.

The appreciation of the US dollar between May 21, 2001 and March 24, 2020, was 181%.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: Dozens of UK cyclosporiasis victims had vacationed at Riviera Maya resorts
World.content:
Mexico is tightening health surveillance at more than a dozen hotels in Cancún and the Riviera Maya after the United Kingdom reported dozens of cases of cyclosporiasis in travelers, most of whom had recently stayed at all‑inclusive resorts in the state of Quintana Roo.

At the same time, Mexican officials are saying the country is not facing a domestic outbreak, nor has it been identified as the source of more than 10,000 laboratory-confirmed cyclosporiasis cases reported in the U.S. and 67 infections in British travelers.

Mensaje del secretario de Salud, David Kershenobich: Es importante mencionar que los casos de ciclosporiasis que existen actualmente en México representan el 0.00002% de la población, lo que significa que no tenemos un brote activo. pic.twitter.com/UN0wC6qmcH — SALUD México (@SSalud_mx) August 6, 2026

The Health Ministry has confirmed 33 cases of cyclosporiasis in 13 Mexican states between May 25 and July 31 and opened investigations into possible links with U.S. and U.K. infection reports.

Health Minister David Kershenobich said in a video posted Thursday that detected cases represent just 0.00002% of Mexico’s population. He also stressed that Cyclospora cayetanensis infections “are recurrent worldwide” and that there is no scientific evidence to date that Mexico is the origin of the outbreak.

The ministry, working with the Federal Commission for Protection against Sanitary Risks (Cofepris) and the General Directorate of Epidemiology (DGE), has deployed five inspection teams to 16 hotels in Quintana Roo.

The inspections follows a July 30 UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) alert reporting 67 cyclosporiasis cases between April 30 and July 15, with 48 of 51 patients who provided travel information reporting trips to Mexico — mainly to the Riviera Maya and Cancún.

UKHSA said the affected travelers stayed in “a range of different hotels” and consumed varied food and drink in all‑inclusive packages — emphasizing that investigations have not identified any single hotel or product as the source.

In response, Mexican inspectors conducted field visits this week in Quintana Roo during which they collected samples of food, water, fruits and vegetables, according to a Ministry of Health press release.

Laboratory analyses are still in process and authorities say results will be released when testing is complete.

Meanwhile, Mexican authorities are cooperating with U.S. counterparts on a multistate outbreak that officials say has sickened more than 10,000 people and is linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms de Mexico, grown in the central state of Guanajuato and distributed to Taco Bell and other outlets.

Product testing has not yielded any confirmed positive samples, though inspections are ongoing.

In tourist zones in Quintana Roo and elsewhere, Mexico’s Health Ministry has expanded surveillance, reinforced food safety protocols and reminded travelers and residents to wash and disinfect fruits and vegetables, drink potable water and seek medical attention for persistent diarrhea, especially after travel.

Officials also stress that identifying a country as a preliminary origin of a product under investigation “does not, in itself, constitute evidence that the contamination occurred in that place,” and say epidemiological work will continue until conclusive findings are available.

Cyclosporiasis is an intestinal infection usually acquired by eating or drinking contaminated food or water. Symptoms include watery “explosive diarrhea,” stomach cramps, nausea, loss of appetite, fatigue and low‑grade fever.

The 33 patients diagnosed in Mexico remain under observation; no deaths linked to the infection have been reported in Mexico.

With reports from El País, Infobae La Silla Rota and El Heraldo de México

World.title: An American is caught fleeing to the US border after fatal shootings in Saltillo
World.content:
A Texas man is accused of murdering three people in the northern state of Coahuila and then fleeing with his 3-year-old son toward the United States, before being arrested while trying to cross the border.

The suspect, identified as Chad Eberle, a former police officer, allegedly shot and killed two women and a man while seriously wounding another woman inside a home in the Espinoza Mireles neighborhood of Saltillo, the Coahuila state capital, on Tuesday afternoon.

The Coahuila Attorney General’s Office (FGE) said the suspect was apprehended at the Piedras Negras border crossing in his gray Chevrolet Silverado around five hours after the shooting.

The child was retrieved uninjured and was placed under the protection of the Office of the Attorney for Children and Families.

According to initial reports, Eberle arrived at 1221 José Espinoza Fuente Street around 3 p.m. Inside were his ex-partner Litzy Mora (26 years old), her sister Laura Jaquelín (22) and their parents Ana Laura (44) and Emanuel (44), as well as 3-year-old Benjamin.

Eberle, who had a restraining order against him due to accusations of domestic violence and was legally prohibited from seeing his son, demanded to see the boy.

ACTUALIZACIÓN | MULTIHOMICIDIO EN SALTILLO La Fiscalía General del Estado informa que, dentro de la Causa Penal 547/2026JEVF, la Autoridad Judicial giró Orden de Aprehensión en contra de Chad N, por su probable responsabilidad en los delitos de feminicidio y homicidio… pic.twitter.com/hBLpZu42FY — Federico Fernández (@FedericoFdzMx) August 5, 2026

When Litzy refused to let him inside the house, Eberle took out a gun and shot all four adults before fleeing with Benjamin.

An hour later, relatives of the victims forced their way into the house and immediately called 911.

Paramedics found Litzy still alive with a gunshot wound to the head and rushed her to a hospital where doctors said she remains in critical condition. The other three members of the family were declared dead at the scene.

The authorities were able to identify the alleged perpetrator and his vehicle by reviewing security camera footage from nearby homes and businesses, and quickly mobilized a manhunt that included state police, FGE agents, the National Guard and both the Army and the Marines.

Within half-an-hour, the suspect was located about 170 kilometers north headed toward the U.S. border. As he had already passed the Castaños, Coahuila, checkpoint, U.S. Customs and Border Patrol was advised of the situation.

State police established a security perimeter as Eberle approached Piedras Negras and notified U.S. officials. When the suspect got to the border, CBP officers assisted in apprehending him.

The 35-year-old former policeman was then handed over to the FGE for prosecution.

With reports from Zócalo, Univision, La Jornada and Milenio

World.title: Department of Environment investigating fish kill in Belize River Valley, public urged to avoid untreated river water
World.content:
Department of Environment investigating fish kill in Belize River Valley, public urged to avoid untreated river water

By Zoila Palma: The Department of the Environment (DOE) is investigating a fish kill reported in the Belize River Valley and has issued a public advisory warning residents not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from affected areas while the investigation continues.

The Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management said the DOE received reports on August 4 of numerous dead fish floating along sections of the Belize River, prompting a multi-agency response.

According to the department, a joint assessment was launched involving Belize Water Services Limited (BWS), the Ministry of Health and Wellness, the National Emergency Management Organization (NEMO), the Fisheries Department, the Ministry of Infrastructure Development and Housing (MIDH), and other relevant agencies.

The release stated that “the Department is actively responding to the ongoing fish kill issue reported in the Belize River Valley area.”

DOE said the exercise included “water quality monitoring and sampling, as well as assessments of land-clearing activities, potential wastewater discharge sources, and other factors that may have contributed to impacts on the aquatic environment.”

As investigations continue, the DOE is advising residents to take precautionary measures.

The department warned the public “not to consume fish or other aquatic resources from the affected areas and not to drink untreated river water or use untreated river water for cooking or food preparation.” It also advised against using untreated river water for livestock or pets until further notice.

The department emphasized that the advisory applies only to untreated water taken directly from the river and does not affect the public water supply.

The release noted that “BWS has confirmed that the water currently being supplied from its Water Treatment Plant remains safe for consumption and meets the required potable water quality standards. There has been no disruption to the continuity of the water supply.”

DOE noted that technical assessments are ongoing to determine the cause of the fish kill and pledged to keep the public informed as new information becomes available.

The DOE also reminded the public that the release of untreated wastewater, or treated effluent that fails to meet environmental standards, is prohibited under Belize’s Environmental Protection Regulations and constitutes an offence.

World.title: The case for Allan Pollard, measured the way a city should measure a mayor
World.content:
The case for Allan Pollard, measured the way a city should measure a mayor

By Horace Palacio:

The People’s United Party will soon ask its Belize City delegates a single question. Who should carry its banner for mayor in 2027, Councillor Allan Pollard Jr. or Deputy Mayor Eluide Miller?

Today I am going to answer that question openly, and make the case for Pollard. But I will make it the way this column has always insisted arguments be made, on the record, with respect for both men, and by a standard bigger than either of them.

Because before we compare two candidates, remember what the prize actually is. Belize City is not a title. It is the largest, hardest job in municipal government in this country. Flooding that swallows streets. Drains that fail. Garbage that piles. Traffic that strangles. Crime that shadows whole neighborhoods. Whoever wins this convention inherits all of it. So the question for delegates is not who do you like. It is who is readiest, this March, for that load.

Measure the two men by that standard, and the case builds itself on four pillars.

Pillar one. The record. Allan Pollard has served the people of Belize City as an elected councillor for eight years, across three terms, including service as deputy mayor. Eluide Miller, a capable young man, has served two. That is not an insult to Miller. It is arithmetic. Pollard has sat through four times the budgets, four times the floods, four times the hard seasons of that council. He has already held the deputy’s chair Miller holds now, and then kept serving. The city’s problems are too old and too heavy for the top job to double as a classroom. Experience is not everything, but in a crisis city, it is not nothing either. It is the difference between learning the machine and driving it.

Pillar two. Character, tested in the dark. Here is the part of Pollard’s story that tells you more than any manifesto. In 2023, he wanted this same candidacy. The party asked him to step aside for unity’s sake. He swallowed his ambition and did it. Reports say the Prime Minister personally assured him his patience would be honored this cycle. Now, let me be precise about why this matters, because it is not the reason some think. I have written before that no seat in Belize should be awarded by turn, only by merit, and I stand by every word. Pollard does not deserve the candidacy because he waited. He deserves consideration because of what the waiting revealed. A man who can put the team above his own ambition, keep working for three more years without sulking, and return stronger, has shown you his character under the hardest test politics offers, the test of being told no. Most politicians fail that test loudly. Pollard passed it quietly. That is the temperament you want holding a city’s purse and pressure.

Pillar three. Whose hands hold him. Look carefully at the two campaign launches, because launches are confessions. Miller announced flanked by seven fellow councillors, the establishment closing ranks, with the outgoing mayor reportedly grooming him as successor. Pollard arrived with no councillors at all, just a crowd of ordinary city people, family, friends, supporters he did not have to summon. One candidacy was born in the council chamber. The other was born on the street. And a mayor, understand, does not answer to the chamber. He answers to the street. Give me the candidate the people carry over the candidate the machine crowns, every single time. It is also worth noting what Pollard said about that machine, that he wants the door open to new faces, talented people, older, younger, business people, and that whoever the delegates elect to the slate gets his full backing. That is a builder’s posture, not a boss’s.

Pillar four. The money question. There is a figure floating around this race, two hundred dollars per delegate, the whispered price of convention support. I wrote months ago that free is the most expensive thing in Belize, that every bought vote is a purchase the politician later recoups from the public. So hear what Pollard put on the record when the figure was raised. He does not pay for delegates. His relationships with them were built over years of showing up, and, in his words, that is something money cannot buy. A candidate who refuses to buy his way in owes nothing on his way up. That single stance, publicly planted, is worth more to this city than any promise on any flyer. And let me be crystal clear in fairness, no evidence before me says Miller pays for delegates, and I make no such claim. I simply issue the challenge this column must issue. Mr. Miller, plant the same flag, publicly, and let this be the first convention in memory where both camps swear off the wallet and compete on the work.

Now, the fairness Miller is owed, because this endorsement will not be built on his burial.

Eluide Miller has done something in this race that deserves genuine applause. When party heavyweights reportedly leaned on him to step aside and clear the path, he refused, and insisted the delegates decide. That is democratic spine, and it is exactly what I have preached in these pages, conventions over coronations, always. Both camps, let us be honest, have maneuvered behind the scenes in this contest, which is precisely why the convention itself is the clean answer. Miller is young, described even by neutrals in the party as energetic and creative, and if he loses this race well, his future in city politics is real. The party leader himself says both men have talent, and he is right.

But talent is the entry fee, not the verdict. The verdict comes from the standard we set at the start. Which man, this March, is readiest for the hardest municipal job in Belize?

Eight years against two. A deputy mayor’s chair already held, then exceeded. Ambition tested by sacrifice and passed. A campaign carried by the street rather than crowned by the chamber. And a public refusal to purchase what should only be earned. On the record before the delegates, that is Allan Pollard’s case, and it is a strong one.

So to the delegates who will file into that convention, I close with this. You hold a privilege thousands of city residents wish they held. Do not sell it, to anyone. Do not lend it to pressure, from anyone. Weigh the records, question both men hard, and choose the readiest hands.

Weighed that way, honestly and without malice, my case is made.

The city’s next chapter should be written by the man who spent eight years learning to hold the pen.

The views expressed in this article are those of the author, Horace Palacio, and do not necessarily reflect the views or editorial stance of Breaking Belize News.

World.title: Prime Minister meets with stakeholders in sugar industry to discuss mealbug infestation
World.content:
Prime Minister meets with stakeholders in sugar industry to discuss mealbug infestation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Prime Minister John Briceno met with stakeholders in the sugar industry to discuss the mealbug infestation.

In addition, the PM also received updates on two important initiatives —CRESAP and the Building the Adaptive Capacity of Sugarcane Farmers in Northern Belize (BAC-SuF) Project.

The PM explained that financed by the Green Climate Fund and implemented by the Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (5Cs), BAC-SuF is helping to strengthen the resilience of our sugarcane farmers and safeguard the future of this vital industry.

World.title: Cabinet Approves Amendments to Cybercrime Bill to safeguard freedom of expression
World.content:
Cabinet Approves Amendments to Cybercrime Bill to safeguard freedom of expression

By Zoila Palma: Cabinet has approved amendments to the Cybercrime Bill aimed at clarifying the scope of offences while ensuring the legislation aligns with constitutional protections for freedom of expression.

According to the Cabinet statement, the changes are intended to preserve the Government’s ability to prosecute serious forms of technology-facilitated abuse, including malicious deepfakes, online impersonation, extortion, threats, and targeted harassment.

At the same time, the amendments seek to safeguard freedom of expression, political debate, journalism, satire, and public accountability.

As part of this safeguard, the cabinet release notes that the DPP’s written consent will be required before the prosecution of an offence can occur.

This latest revision comes after concerns were raised by media organizations, civil society groups, and members of the public that earlier provisions of the Cybercrime Bill could have had unintended consequences for free speech and press freedom.

World.title: Cabinet approves US $8 million loan from Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for efficiency of wage bill
World.content:
Cabinet approves US $8 million loan from Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for efficiency of wage bill

By Zoila Palma: During Cabinet’s meeting on July 28th and August 4th, 2026, the Government of Belize approved entering into a loan agreement with the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) for US$8 million.

According to the cabinet release, the loan will be used to “improve the efficiency of the Central Government’s wage bill and to increase the efficacy of strategic public employment”.

The funding is expected to help improve the allocation of public resources, promote more efficient staffing across government ministries and departments, and support efforts to modernize public sector management.

The project carries a total value of US$9 million, or roughly BZ$18 million, made up of the US$8 million in IDB financing and US$1 million in local counterpart funding, and is to be implemented over a five-year disbursement period.

World.title: Cabinet approves 20.9 million dollar investment in electric buses and charging infrastructure
World.content:
Cabinet approves 20.9 million dollar investment in electric buses and charging infrastructure

By Zoila Palma: During Cabinet’s session on July 28th and August 4th, 2026, the Government of Belize approved the change of its planned investment in the National Bus Company (NBC) from “terminals to electric buses and related charging infrastructure with a value of approximately BZ$20.9 million”.

The decision will require a revised Public Transportation Investment Bill to reflect this change.

The revision will include a proposed long-term lease agreement under which the Government would lease the bus terminals to the NBC.

The move forms part of the Government’s efforts to modernize Belize’s public transportation system through the introduction of electric buses and supporting infrastructure.

World.title: Youth Shadow Mayor Begins Leadership Journey at Belize City Hall
World.content:
Youth Shadow Mayor Begins Leadership Journey at Belize City Hall

By Zoila Palma: Youth Shadow Mayor Caitlin Aragon officially began her leadership experience with the Belize City Council after being welcomed by Mayor Bernard Wagner during an introductory visit to City Hall.

As part of the visit, Aragon toured the Office of the Mayor and learned about the daily responsibilities of the Mayor’s Office and the Belize City Council’s role in serving residents and guiding the city’s development.

The initiative provides mentorship and hands-on exposure to local government, giving the Youth Shadow Mayor valuable insight into leadership and public service

World.title: Blue Teddy Bear Campaign launches teacher training to strengthen Child Protection in Belize
World.content:
Blue Teddy Bear Campaign launches teacher training to strengthen Child Protection in Belize

By Zoila Palma: The Blue Teddy Bear Campaign has launched Phase II of its national child protection initiative, expanding its efforts to equip teachers, parents, and students with the knowledge and skills needed to create safer environments for children across Belize. The new phase officially began today with teacher training sessions aimed at strengthening child safeguarding practices in schools.

The latest training brought together 22 educators from Wesley College, Excelsior High School, and Gwen Lizarraga High School. It followed an earlier session involving 60 teachers from Maud Williams High School, Anglican Cathedral College, and Sadie Vernon Technical High School. With the support of the Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology, a total of 82 teachers will receive training during this phase of the campaign.

Teachers are among the most influential adults in a child’s life and often serve as the first line of defense for vulnerable children. As mandatory reporters under Belize’s child protection framework, educators play a vital role in identifying signs of abuse, taking appropriate action, and ensuring children receive the protection and support they need.

The training focuses on child protection principles, safeguarding measures, recognizing indicators of abuse, reporting obligations, and practical approaches to supporting children who may be at risk. Organizers said strengthening educators’ understanding of these areas will help ensure schools remain safe spaces where children can learn, grow, and thrive.

The Blue Teddy Bear Campaign is a partnership between the National Commission for Families and Children (NCFC), UNICEF Belize, the Ministry of Human Development, Family Support and Gender Affairs, and the Office of the Special Envoy for the Development of Families and Children. Since its launch, the campaign has promoted awareness and action to eliminate violence, abuse, and exploitation of children. Phase II builds on those efforts by focusing on adults and institutions that play a central role in children’s daily lives, reinforcing the message that protecting children is a shared national responsibility.

World.title: Card, Douglas win silver in 100m at World U20 Championships
World.content:
Jamaica's Shanoya Douglas parades with the Jamaican flag after winning the silver medal in the women's 100m on Thursday's second day of the 2026 World Athletics Under 20 championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon. Douglas, the world leader was beaten by American Maria Maxwell. (Photos: Paul Reid)

OREGON, USA — Jamaica’s Gary Card and Shanoya Douglas won silver medals in the men and women’s 100m on Thursday night at the World Athletics Under-20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon.

It was the first medals for Jamaica at the championships, putting them in ninth position on the medals tables.

Americans Tate Taylor and Mia Maxwell delighted the home fans by winning the double, only the second time athletes from the same country had taken both gold medals at the same under-20 championships after Americans Noah Lyles and Candace Hill achieved the feat in 2016 in Bydgoszcz, Poland.

Card got off to a fast start but was chased and caught by Tate who passed him to win in a personal best 9.94 seconds (0.1m/s), the Jamaican second in 10.05 seconds. South Africa’s Marko Ferreira took the bronze with 10.16 seconds.

Maxwell got the edge over Douglas at the start and held off the Jamaican to the tape, running 11.14 seconds (-0.1m/s). Douglas finished second in 11.17 seconds with Italy’s Kelly Ann Maevane Doualla Edimo third in 11.27 seconds. Theianna-Lee Terrelonge was sixth in 11.37 seconds

It was the first time in 10 years an American won the women’s 100m and snapped the four-championships winning streak by the Jamaicans – Briana Williams in 2018, Tina Clayton in 2021 and 2022 and Alana Reid in 2024.

Also on Thursday, thrower Able Mills failed to record a legal throw in both the women’s discus and shot put finals that were held within two hours of each other.

Mills had thrown distances close to her lifetime bests to qualify for both finals but failed to make a legal mark in either.

Jamaica also failed to qualify any runner in the 400m finals set for Friday afternoon, all four failing to get past their semifinals.

Jabari Matheson who was running his fourth 400m race in two days, placed sixth in his semi-final in 47.29 seconds, the first time he failed to go under the 47.00 second mark at the championships.

Jason Pitter failed to get up to his high standards, and was sixth in his semi-final in 46.50 seconds after he advanced on time from the first round.

Daniellia Dixon was fifth in her semi-final in 53.77 seconds and Shameika McLean, who had run three times since the start of the championships, just failed to get into the final after placing fourth in her semis in 54.24 seconds.

-Paul A Reid
